mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of simple harmonic motion?
options: The motion of a simple pendulum
The motion of a ceiling fan
The spinning of the Earth on its axis
A bouncing ball on a floor
mcqs.why: The book lists the motion of a simple pendulum as simple harmonic motion: it swings to and fro about a mean position under a restoring force. A ceiling fan and the spinning Earth rotate continuously in one direction, and a bouncing ball is not in SHM.

mcqs.q: If the mass of the bob of a pendulum is increased by a factor of 3, the period of the pendulum's motion will
options: Be increased by a factor of 2
Be decreased by a factor of 2
Be decreased by a factor of 4
mcqs.why: The time period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length and on g, not on the mass of the bob. Tripling the mass therefore leaves the period unchanged.

mcqs.q: Which of the following devices can be used to produce both transverse and longitudinal waves?
mcqs.why: A helical spring (slinky) can be shaken side to side to make transverse waves and pushed and pulled along its length to make longitudinal waves, so it produces both types.

mcqs.q: Waves transfer
mcqs.why: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Frequency, wavelength and velocity are properties of the wave, not things it transfers.

mcqs.q: Conduction, radiation and wave motion are all examples of
mcqs.why: The book's question lists conduction, radiation and wave motion together as methods by which energy is transferred from one place to another.

mcqs.q: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves have the same
mcqs.why: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, the speed of light. Their frequencies and wavelengths differ from one type to another, which is why v = f x wavelength still holds for each of them.

mcqs.q: A vibrator working at 30 Hz produces 25 complete waves in a distance of 50 cm. What is the wavelength of the waves?
mcqs.why: Wavelength = total distance / number of waves = 50 / 25 = 2 cm. The 25 waves together occupy 50 cm, so each single wave is 2 cm long.

mcqs.q: For the same ripple tank waves (frequency 30 Hz, wavelength 2 cm), the velocity of the wave is
mcqs.why: Velocity v = f x wavelength = 30 x 2 = 60 cm/s. The wavelength is 50 / 25 = 2 cm, and multiplying by the frequency 30 Hz gives the speed.

mcqs.q: Which characteristic of a wave is independent of the others?
mcqs.why: Speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by v = f x wavelength, so changing one affects the others. Amplitude depends only on how strongly the source vibrates and is independent of the rest.

mcqs.q: The relation between v, f and wavelength of a wave is
mcqs.why: In one time period the wave travels one wavelength, so v = wavelength / T, and since f = 1 / T this becomes v = f x wavelength.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
10.1. What is simple harmonic motion? What are the necessary conditions for a body to execute simple harmonic motion?

Simple harmonic motion is the to-and-fro motion of a body about a mean position in which its acceleration is always directed towards the mean position and is proportional to its displacement from it. The necessary conditions are: a restoring force must act on the body, this force must always point towards the mean position, and its magnitude must increase as the displacement from the mean position increases.

10.2. Think of several examples of motion in everyday life that are simple harmonic.

Everyday examples of simple harmonic motion are the swing of a simple pendulum in a clock, the vibrations of a guitar string, the motion of a mass hanging from a spring, the motion of a ball rolling in a bowl, and the vibrations of a tuning fork. In each case the body moves to and fro about a fixed mean position under a restoring force.

10.3. What are damped oscillations? How does damping progressively reduce the amplitude of oscillation?

Damped oscillations are oscillations whose amplitude decreases gradually with time because of resistive forces such as friction and air resistance. In every vibration some energy is used up in overcoming these resistances, so less energy remains for the next vibration. As the energy of oscillation falls, the amplitude also falls, until the motion finally stops.

10.4. How can you define the term wave? Elaborate the difference between mechanical and electromagnetic waves. Give examples of each.

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Mechanical waves need a material medium for their travel, for example sound waves and water waves. Electromagnetic waves do not need any medium and can travel through vacuum, for example light waves, radio waves and X-rays.

10.5. Distinguish between longitudinal and transverse waves with suitable examples.

In a transverse wave the particles of the medium vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel of the wave, for example waves on a rope and light waves. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions, for example sound waves and waves in a slinky spring.

10.6. Draw a transverse wave with an amplitude of 2 cm and a wavelength of 4 cm. Label a crest and trough on the wave.

Draw a smooth sine-shaped wave on a horizontal axis. Mark the highest points as crests and the lowest points as troughs. The vertical distance from the middle line to a crest is 2 cm, which is the amplitude. The horizontal distance between two neighbouring crests is 4 cm, which is the wavelength.

10.7. Derive a relationship between velocity, frequency and wavelength of a wave. Write a formula relating velocity of a wave to its time period and wavelength.

In one time period T a wave travels one wavelength, so its velocity is v = wavelength / T. Since frequency f = 1 / T, this becomes v = f x wavelength. In terms of time period alone, the relation is v = wavelength / T, where wavelength is the distance between two neighbouring crests.

10.8. Waves are the means of energy transfer without transfer of matter. Justify this statement with the help of a simple experiment.

Place a cork on the surface of water in a ripple tank and produce waves at one end. The cork moves up and down at its own place as each wave passes, but it does not travel forward with the wave. This shows that the wave carries energy forward and makes the cork vibrate, while the water particles themselves do not travel with the wave.

10.9. Explain the following properties of waves with reference to ripple tank experiment: a. Reflection b. Refraction c. Diffraction

Reflection: when straight waves in a ripple tank strike a flat barrier they bounce back, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. Refraction: when waves pass from deep to shallow water their speed and wavelength decrease and their direction bends, while frequency stays the same. Diffraction: when waves pass through a narrow gap or round an edge they spread out into the shadow region behind the obstacle.

10.10. Does increasing the frequency of a wave also increase its wavelength? If not, how are these quantities related?

No, increasing the frequency does not increase the wavelength. For a wave travelling at a fixed speed, v = f x wavelength, so frequency and wavelength are inversely related. When frequency increases, wavelength decreases in the same proportion, and their product remains equal to the wave speed.

Directed towards the mean position and proportional to the displacement from it
Proportional to the velocity of the body
mcqs.why: Simple harmonic motion is to-and-fro motion about a mean position in which the acceleration is always directed towards the mean position and is proportional to the displacement from it.

options: A constant force acting in one direction
A restoring force that points towards the mean position and grows as displacement increases
A force that pushes the body away from the mean position
mcqs.why: The conditions for SHM are that a restoring force acts on the body, it always points towards the mean position, and its magnitude increases as the displacement from the mean position increases.

mcqs.q: Damped oscillations are oscillations in which
options: The frequency increases gradually with time
The amplitude increases gradually with time
The time period keeps on decreasing
The amplitude decreases gradually with time because of resistive forces
mcqs.why: In damped oscillations, friction and air resistance use up some energy in every vibration, so less energy remains for the next one and the amplitude falls gradually until the motion stops.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches a wave type with an example?
options: Mechanical wave — sound wave; electromagnetic wave — light wave
Mechanical wave — light wave; electromagnetic wave — sound wave
Mechanical wave — X-rays; electromagnetic wave — water wave
Mechanical wave — radio wave; electromagnetic wave — sound wave
mcqs.why: Mechanical waves such as sound and water waves need a material medium. Electromagnetic waves such as light, radio waves and X-rays need no medium and can travel through vacuum.

mcqs.q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate
options: Along the direction of travel of the wave
At right angles to the direction of travel of the wave
In circles around their mean positions
mcqs.why: In a transverse wave, for example waves on a rope or light waves, the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels.

mcqs.q: A longitudinal wave travels through a medium by forming
mcqs.why: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of travel, crowding together in compressions and spreading apart in rarefactions, as in sound waves and waves in a slinky spring.

mcqs.why: In one time period T a wave travels exactly one wavelength, so its velocity is v = wavelength / T, which with f = 1 / T gives v = f x wavelength.

mcqs.q: A cork floating on water in a ripple tank moves up and down but does not travel with the waves. This experiment shows that waves
options: Carry the water particles along with them
Stop at the surface of the water
mcqs.why: The cork vibrates at its own place as each wave passes but does not move forward, proving the wave carries energy forward while the water particles themselves do not travel with it.

mcqs.q: When plane waves in a ripple tank pass from deep water to shallow water,
options: Their frequency decreases while speed stays the same
Their speed and wavelength decrease while frequency stays the same
Their speed increases and wavelength increases
mcqs.why: In refraction in a ripple tank, waves entering shallow water slow down and their wavelength decreases in the same proportion, while the frequency, fixed by the vibrator, remains unchanged.

mcqs.q: For a wave travelling at fixed speed, if the frequency is increased, the wavelength
mcqs.why: From v = f x wavelength, frequency and wavelength are inversely related at fixed speed: when frequency increases, wavelength decreases in the same proportion so their product stays equal to the speed.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
10.1. If the length of a simple pendulum is doubled, what will be the change in its time period?

The time period of a simple pendulum is T = 2 x pi x square root (length / g), so T is proportional to the square root of the length. Doubling the length multiplies T by the square root of 2, that is about 1.41 times. The new time period is therefore about 1.41 times the old time period.

10.2. A ball is dropped from a certain height onto the floor and keeps bouncing. Is the motion of the ball simple harmonic? Explain.

No, the bouncing ball is not in simple harmonic motion. Although it moves up and down repeatedly, its acceleration is not proportional to its displacement from a mean position and is not always directed towards that position. Between bounces it falls freely under gravity, and the motion is interrupted at each impact, so the conditions for simple harmonic motion are not met.

10.3. A student performed two experiments with a simple pendulum using bobs of different masses, keeping other parameters constant. The time period did not change. Why?

The time period of a simple pendulum, T = 2 x pi x square root (length / g), does not contain the mass of the bob. A heavier bob experiences a larger restoring force, but it also has larger inertia, and the two effects cancel exactly. The time period therefore depends only on the length and on g, not on the mass.

10.4. What types of waves do not require any material medium for their propagation?

Electromagnetic waves do not require any material medium. They are produced by vibrating electric charges and consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, so they can travel through vacuum. Examples are light, radio waves, microwaves, infrared rays, ultraviolet rays, X-rays and gamma rays.

10.5. Plane waves in the ripple tank undergo refraction when they move from deep to shallow water. What change occurs in the speed of the waves?

When waves move from deep water into shallow water their speed decreases. The wavelength also decreases in the same proportion, while the frequency remains unchanged. Because the speed changes, the direction of the waves bends at the boundary, which is refraction.

mcqs.q: A ball dropped onto the floor keeps bouncing. Its motion is not simple harmonic because
options: It moves up and down repeatedly
It loses height after every bounce
Gravity acts on it all the time
Its acceleration is not proportional to its displacement from a mean position and the motion is interrupted at each impact
mcqs.why: Between bounces the ball falls freely under gravity and each impact interrupts the motion, so the acceleration is neither proportional to the displacement nor always directed towards a mean position, as SHM requires.

mcqs.q: Two pendulums with bobs of different masses have the same time period (other things equal) because
options: The time period formula T = 2 x pi x square root (length / g) contains no mass term
A heavier bob swings faster and cancels its extra weight
Air resistance is the same on both bobs
The length of both pendulums changes with mass
mcqs.why: A heavier bob experiences a larger restoring force but also has larger inertia, and the two effects cancel exactly. The period depends only on length and g, not on mass.

mcqs.why: Electromagnetic waves are produced by vibrating electric charges and consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, so they can travel through vacuum. Examples are light, radio waves, microwaves, X-rays and gamma rays.

mcqs.q: When plane waves in a ripple tank move from deep water into shallow water, their speed
mcqs.why: Waves slow down in shallow water. Their wavelength decreases in the same proportion, the frequency stays the same, and the change of speed bends their direction, which is refraction.

mcqs.q: The time period of a simple pendulum is proportional to
options: The square root of its length
mcqs.why: From T = 2 x pi x square root (l / g), the period grows only as the square root of the length: quadrupling the length only doubles the period.

mcqs.q: If the length of a simple pendulum is made four times, its time period will become
mcqs.why: T is proportional to the square root of l. The square root of 4 is 2, so making the length four times multiplies the period by 2.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves consist of
mcqs.why: Electromagnetic waves are produced by vibrating electric charges and are made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which is why they need no material medium.

mcqs.why: The frequency is fixed by the source and cannot change at the boundary. The speed and wavelength both decrease in the same proportion, and the direction bends.

mcqs.q: The bending of waves at the boundary between deep and shallow water is called
mcqs.why: Because the speed changes at the boundary, the waves change direction there. This bending of waves due to a change of speed is refraction.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
10.1. The time period of a simple pendulum is 2 s. What will be its length on the Earth? What will be its length on the Moon if g on Moon = g on Earth / 6, where g on Earth = 10 m/s^2?

Step 1: Use T = 2 x pi x square root (l / g), so l = g x T^2 / (4 x pi^2).

Step 2: On Earth: l = 10 x (2)^2 / (4 x 3.14^2) = 40 / 39.48 = 1.01 m, about 1.02 m.

Step 3: On the Moon g = 10 / 6 = 1.67 m/s^2, so l = 1.67 x 4 / 39.48 = 0.17 m.

Final answer: Length on Earth = 1.02 m; length on Moon = 0.17 m.

10.2. A pendulum of length 0.99 m is taken to the Moon by an astronaut. The period of the pendulum is 4.9 s. What is the value of g on the surface of the Moon?

Step 1: From T = 2 x pi x square root (l / g), we get g = 4 x pi^2 x l / T^2.

Step 2: Substitute l = 0.99 m and T = 4.9 s: g = 4 x (3.14)^2 x 0.99 / (4.9)^2.

Step 3: g = 39.48 x 0.99 / 24.01 = 39.09 / 24.01 = 1.63 m/s^2.

Final answer: g on the Moon = 1.63 m/s^2.

10.3. Find the time periods of a simple pendulum of 1 metre length, placed on Earth and on Moon. The value of g on the surface of Moon is 1/6 of its value on Earth, where g on Earth is 10 m/s^2.

Step 1: Use T = 2 x pi x square root (l / g) with l = 1 m.

Step 2: On Earth: T = 2 x 3.14 x square root (1 / 10) = 6.28 x 0.316 = 1.99 s, about 2 s.

Step 3: On the Moon g = 10 / 6 = 1.67 m/s^2, so T = 6.28 x square root (1 / 1.67) = 6.28 x 0.774 = 4.86 s, about 4.9 s.

Final answer: Time period on Earth = 2 s; on Moon = 4.9 s.

10.4. A simple pendulum completes one vibration in two seconds. Calculate its length, when g = 10.0 m/s^2.

Step 1: Time period T = 2 s and l = g x T^2 / (4 x pi^2).

Step 2: l = 10 x (2)^2 / (4 x 3.14^2) = 40 / 39.48.

Step 3: l = 1.01 m, about 1.02 m.

Final answer: Length = 1.02 m.

10.5. If 100 waves pass through a point of a medium in 20 seconds, what is the frequency and the time period of the wave? If its wavelength is 6 cm, calculate the wave speed.

Step 1: Frequency f = number of waves / time = 100 / 20 = 5 Hz.

Step 2: Time period T = 1 / f = 1 / 5 = 0.2 s.

Step 3: Wavelength = 6 cm = 0.06 m. Wave speed v = f x wavelength = 5 x 0.06 = 0.3 m/s.

Final answer: Frequency = 5 Hz, time period = 0.2 s, wave speed = 0.3 m/s.

10.6. A wooden bar vibrating into the water surface in a ripple tank has a frequency of 12 Hz. The resulting wave has a wavelength of 3 cm. What is the speed of the wave?

Step 1: Wavelength = 3 cm = 0.03 m and frequency f = 12 Hz.

Step 2: Wave speed v = f x wavelength = 12 x 0.03.

Step 3: v = 0.36 m/s.

Final answer: Speed of the wave = 0.36 m/s.

10.7. A transverse wave produced on a spring has a frequency of 190 Hz and travels along the length of the spring of 90 m, in 0.5 s. (a) What is the period of the wave? (b) What is the speed of the wave? (c) What is the wavelength of the wave?

Step 1: Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 190 = 0.0053 s, about 0.01 s to one significant figure.

Step 2: Speed v = distance / time = 90 / 0.5 = 180 m/s.

Step 3: Wavelength = v / f = 180 / 190 = 0.95 m.

Final answer: Period = 0.01 s, speed = 180 m/s, wavelength = 0.95 m.

10.8. Water waves in a shallow dish are 6.0 cm long. At one point, the water moves up and down at a rate of 4.8 oscillations per second. (a) What is the speed of the water waves? (b) What is the period of the water waves?

Step 1: Frequency f = 4.8 Hz and wavelength = 6.0 cm = 0.06 m.

Step 2: Speed v = f x wavelength = 4.8 x 0.06 = 0.288 m/s, about 0.29 m/s.

Step 3: Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 4.8 = 0.208 s, about 0.21 s.

Final answer: Speed = 0.29 m/s, period = 0.21 s.

10.9. At one end of a ripple tank 80 cm across, a 5 Hz vibrator produces waves whose wavelength is 40 mm. Find the time the waves need to cross the tank.

Step 1: Wavelength = 40 mm = 0.04 m and frequency f = 5 Hz.

Step 2: Wave speed v = f x wavelength = 5 x 0.04 = 0.2 m/s.

Step 3: Distance = 80 cm = 0.8 m. Time = distance / speed = 0.8 / 0.2 = 4 s.

Final answer: Time to cross the tank = 4 s.

10.10. What is the wavelength of the radiowaves transmitted by an FM station at 90 MHz? Where 1 M = 10^6, and speed of radiowave is 3 x 10^8 m/s.

Step 1: Frequency f = 90 MHz = 90 x 10^6 Hz = 9 x 10^7 Hz.

Step 2: Wavelength = speed / frequency = (3 x 10^8) / (9 x 10^7).

Step 3: Wavelength = 3.33 m.

Final answer: Wavelength = 3.33 m.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a longitudinal wave?
mcqs.why: In sound, the air particles vibrate along the direction of travel of the wave, forming compressions and rarefactions, so sound is a longitudinal wave. Light and radiowaves are transverse electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.q: Sound travels from its source to your ear
options: By vibrations in wires or strings
mcqs.why: The vibrating source produces alternate compressions and rarefactions, that is, changes in air pressure, which travel through the air to the ear.

mcqs.q: Sound is a form of which kind of energy?
mcqs.why: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and needs a material medium, so it is a form of mechanical energy, unlike electrical, thermal or chemical energy.

mcqs.q: Astronauts in space communicate with each other by radio links because
options: Sound waves cannot travel in space
Sound waves travel very slowly in space
Sound waves travel very fast in space
Sound waves have low frequency in space
mcqs.why: Space is a vacuum with no material medium, and sound, being a mechanical wave, cannot travel through it. Radio waves are electromagnetic and cross the vacuum easily.

mcqs.q: The loudness of a sound is most closely related to its
mcqs.why: Loudness depends mainly on the amplitude of vibration: a larger amplitude carries more energy and produces a louder sound. Frequency governs pitch, not loudness.

mcqs.q: For a normal person, the audible frequency range for sound lies between
mcqs.why: The normal human ear can hear sounds from 20 Hz up to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound and those above 20 kHz are ultrasound.

mcqs.q: When the frequency of a sound wave is increased at fixed speed, which quantities decrease?
mcqs.why: At fixed speed, wavelength = speed / frequency and period = 1 / frequency, so both wavelength and period decrease when frequency increases. Amplitude is independent of frequency.

mcqs.q: If the frequency of a sound wave is doubled, its time period becomes
mcqs.why: Period T = 1 / f. Doubling f gives T = 1 / (2f), which is half the original period.

mcqs.q: At a fixed wave speed, doubling the frequency of a sound wave makes its wavelength
mcqs.why: Wavelength = speed / frequency. With speed fixed, doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.

mcqs.q: The amplitude of a sound wave is independent of its
mcqs.why: The book's explanation states that amplitude is independent of frequency: changing the frequency changes wavelength and period but leaves the amplitude, and hence the loudness, unaffected.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
11.1. What is the necessary condition for the production of sound?

The necessary condition for the production of sound is a vibrating body. Whenever a body vibrates, it disturbs the particles of the medium around it, and these vibrations travel outwards as sound waves. Without vibration, no sound is produced.

11.2. What is the effect of the medium on the speed of sound? In which medium does sound travel faster: air, solid or liquid? Justify your answer.

The speed of sound depends on the medium: it is greatest in solids, less in liquids and least in gases. This is because particles in a solid are packed closely and are strongly linked, so a vibration is passed on very quickly from particle to particle. In air the particles are far apart, so the vibration is transferred more slowly.

11.3. How can you prove the mechanical nature of sound by a simple experiment?

Place an electric bell inside a glass bell jar connected to a vacuum pump and ring the bell. As air is pumped out, the sound becomes fainter and finally cannot be heard, although the bell is still ringing. This proves that sound needs a material medium and is therefore a mechanical wave.

11.4. What do you understand by the longitudinal wave? Describe the longitudinal nature of sound waves.

A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate along the direction of travel of the wave. Sound is a longitudinal wave because a vibrating source produces alternate compressions, where air particles are crowded together, and rarefactions, where they are spread apart, and these regions travel forward through the air.

11.5. Sound is a form of wave. List at least three reasons to support the idea that sound is a wave.

Sound is a wave because it shows reflection, as in an echo; it shows refraction, as sound bends when passing between layers of air at different temperatures; and it shows diffraction, as sound is heard round corners although the source cannot be seen. It also carries energy without carrying matter, which is the defining property of a wave.

11.6. We know that waves manifest phenomenon of reflection, refraction and diffraction. Does sound also manifest these characteristics?

Yes, sound shows all three properties. Reflection of sound is heard as an echo when sound strikes a distant wall. Refraction of sound occurs when sound passes from one layer of air to another of different temperature and bends. Diffraction of sound is observed when sound spreads round a corner or through a doorway into a room.

11.7. What is the difference between the loudness and intensity of sound? Derive the relationship between the two.

Intensity is a physical quantity: the sound energy passing per second through unit area, measured in watts per square metre. Loudness is the sensation felt by the ear and depends on intensity and on the sensitivity of the ear. Loudness L is related to intensity I by L = 10 x log (I / I0), where I0 is the threshold intensity of hearing, so loudness grows only logarithmically with intensity.

11.8. On what factors does the loudness of sound depend?

Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration of the source: larger amplitude gives louder sound. It also depends on the distance from the source, because intensity falls as distance increases. It further depends on the area of the vibrating surface, the density of the medium, and the sensitivity of the listener's ear.

11.9. What do you mean by the term intensity level of the sound? Name and define the unit of intensity level of sound.

Intensity level is a measure of sound intensity on a logarithmic scale, defined as 10 times the logarithm of the ratio of the intensity to the threshold intensity. Its unit is the decibel (dB). One decibel is one-tenth of a bel, and the bel is defined so that an intensity ten times the threshold gives an intensity level of 1 bel, or 10 dB.

11.10. What are the units of loudness? Why do we use logarithmic scale to describe the range of the sound intensities we hear?

Loudness is measured in decibels (dB), and also in phons for the sensation of loudness. We use a logarithmic scale because the human ear responds to an enormous range of intensities, from 10^-12 W/m^2 to about 1 W/m^2, a range of a trillion times. A logarithmic scale compresses this huge range into manageable numbers from 0 dB to about 120 dB.

11.11. What is difference between frequency and pitch? Describe their relationship graphically.

Frequency is a physical quantity: the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz. Pitch is the sensation by which the ear judges a sound as high or low. Pitch increases as frequency increases, roughly in a logarithmic way. On a graph of pitch against frequency, the curve rises steeply at low frequencies and flattens at high frequencies, showing that equal ratios of frequency give equal steps in pitch.

11.12. Describe the effect of change in amplitude on loudness and the effect of change in frequency on pitch of sound.

Increasing the amplitude of a sound wave increases its loudness, because a larger amplitude carries more energy and produces a stronger sensation in the ear. Increasing the frequency increases the pitch, so the sound is heard as higher or shriller. Amplitude does not change pitch, and frequency does not by itself change loudness.

11.13. If the pitch of sound is increased, what are the changes in the following?

a. the frequency b. the wavelength c. the wave velocity d. the amplitude of the wave When pitch increases: (a) the frequency increases, because pitch depends on frequency. (b) The wavelength decreases, because wavelength = speed / frequency at a fixed speed. (c) The wave velocity stays the same, because it depends on the medium, not on the source. (d) The amplitude does not change unless the source is struck harder, so it remains unchanged.

11.14. If we clap or speak in front of a building while standing at a particular distance, we rehear our sound after sometime. Can you explain how does this happen?

This is an echo, caused by reflection of sound. The sound travels to the building, reflects from its wall, and returns to the ear after a short time.

The time delay equals twice the distance to the building divided by the speed of sound. An echo is heard as a distinct sound only if the reflecting surface is at least about 17 metres away.

11.15. What is the audible frequency range for human ear? Does this range vary with the age of people? Explain.

The audible frequency range for a normal human ear is from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Yes, this range changes with age: children can hear frequencies near 20,000 Hz, but with increasing age the upper limit falls, so older people often cannot hear high-frequency sounds. Hearing loss from loud noise also reduces the upper limit.

11.16. Explain that noise is a nuisance.

Noise is unwanted, unpleasant sound that disturbs work, rest and communication. It causes annoyance, loss of concentration, difficulty in sleeping, and stress. Prolonged exposure to loud noise can damage hearing permanently. For these reasons noise is regarded as a form of pollution and a nuisance in homes, schools, hospitals and workplaces.

11.17. Describe the importance of acoustic protection.

Acoustic protection means reducing unwanted sound by soundproofing walls, using double-glazed windows, fitting soft carpets and curtains, and planting trees around buildings. It is important in hospitals, schools, libraries and recording studios, where quiet is needed, and in factories, where it protects workers' hearing and health.

11.18. What are the uses of ultrasound in medicine?

Ultrasound is used in medicine for imaging internal organs without surgery, as in scans of a baby before birth. It is used to examine the heart, liver and kidneys, to break kidney stones, to clean teeth, and to measure blood flow. Because it does not use harmful radiation, it is safe for repeated use.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
11.1. Why are two tin cans with a string stretched between them a better way to communicate than merely shouting through the air?

The stretched string carries vibrations directly from one can to the other with little loss of energy, whereas sound shouted through air spreads in all directions and loses intensity quickly. The string also guides the vibrations along one path, so the sound arrives clearer and louder at the other end.

11.2. We can recognize persons speaking with the same loudness from their voice. How is this possible?

Every person's voice has a different quality, or timbre, because their vocal cords produce a different mixture of overtones along with the main note. Even when two voices have the same loudness and pitch, the ear recognises the different pattern of overtones, which gives each voice its own character.

11.3. You can listen to your friend round a corner, but you cannot watch him/her. Why?

Sound waves have long wavelengths, comparable to the size of doorways and corners, so they diffract strongly and spread round the corner. Light waves have extremely short wavelengths, so they hardly diffract at all and travel in straight lines. The sound therefore reaches your ear round the corner, while the light cannot reach your eye.

11.4. Why must the volume of a stereo in a room with wall-to-wall carpet be tuned higher than in a room with a wooden floor?

Carpet is a soft, porous material that absorbs sound energy, so less sound is reflected back into the room. A wooden floor reflects most of the sound, keeping the room louder. To reach the same loudness in the carpeted room, the stereo must therefore be turned up higher to make up for the absorbed energy.

11.5. A student says that the two terms speed and frequency of the wave refer to the same thing. What is your response?

Speed and frequency are different quantities. Speed is how fast the wave disturbance travels through the medium, measured in metres per second. Frequency is how many vibrations pass a point each second, measured in hertz. They are related by speed = frequency x wavelength, but they are not the same thing.

11.6. Two people are listening to the same music at the same distance. They disagree on its loudness. Explain how this could happen.

Loudness is a sensation, not just a physical measurement, and it depends on the listener's ear. The two people may have different hearing sensitivity, for example one may have partial hearing loss. Their ears may also respond differently to different frequencies, so the same intensity level can feel louder to one person than to the other.

11.7. Is there any difference between echo and reflection of sound? Explain.

Reflection of sound is the general phenomenon in which sound bounces back from a surface. An echo is a particular case of reflection in which the reflected sound is heard as a separate, distinct sound after the original sound has ended. An echo is heard only when the reflecting surface is far enough away, about 17 metres or more, for the brain to separate the two sounds.

11.8. Will two separate 50 dB sounds together constitute a 100 dB sound? Explain.

No, two 50 dB sounds together do not make 100 dB. The decibel scale is logarithmic, so adding intensities does not add decibels. Two equal sounds double the intensity, and doubling the intensity raises the level by only about 3 dB, giving about 53 dB in total, not 100 dB.

11.9. Why is ultrasound useful in the medical field?

Ultrasound is useful because it can form images of soft tissues inside the body without cutting and without harmful radiation. Its short wavelength gives fine detail, and it reflects from boundaries between different tissues, allowing doctors to see organs, a developing baby, and blood flow safely and repeatedly.

lessons.notes_html:
11.1. A normal conversation involves sound intensities of about 3.0 x 10^-6 W/m^2. What is the decibel level for this intensity? What is the intensity of the sound for 100 dB?

Step 1: Intensity level beta = 10 x log (I / I0), where I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2.

Step 2: I / I0 = (3.0 x 10^-6) / (10^-12) = 3.0 x 10^6. Log of this is 6.48.

Step 3: Beta = 10 x 6.48 = 64.8 dB.

Step 4: For 100 dB: 100 = 10 x log (I / 10^-12), so log (I / 10^-12) = 10, giving I = 10^-12 x 10^10 = 0.01 W/m^2.

Final answer: Decibel level = 64.8 dB; intensity for 100 dB = 0.01 W/m^2.

11.2. If at Anarkali Bazar Lahore, intensity level of sound is 80 dB, what will be the intensity of sound there?

Step 1: Beta = 10 x log (I / I0) = 80 dB, so log (I / I0) = 8.

Step 2: I / I0 = 10^8, with I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2.

Step 3: I = 10^8 x 10^-12 = 10^-4 W/m^2.

Final answer: Intensity = 10^-4 W/m^2.

11.3. At a particular temperature, the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. If the wavelength of a note is 5 cm, calculate the frequency of the sound wave. Is this frequency in the audible range of the human ear?

Step 1: Wavelength = 5 cm = 0.05 m and speed v = 330 m/s.

Step 2: Frequency f = v / wavelength = 330 / 0.05 = 6600 Hz = 6.6 x 10^3 Hz.

Step 3: The audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and 6600 Hz lies inside it.

Final answer: Frequency = 6.6 x 10^3 Hz; yes, it is audible.

11.4. A doctor counts 72 heartbeats in 1 min. Calculate the frequency and period of the heartbeats.

Step 1: Frequency f = number of beats / time = 72 / 60 s = 1.2 Hz.

Step 2: Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 1.2 = 0.83 s.

Final answer: Frequency = 1.2 Hz, period = 0.83 s.

11.5. A marine survey ship sends a sound wave straight to the seabed. It receives an echo 1.5 s later. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. Find the depth of the sea at this position.

Step 1: The sound travels down to the seabed and back, so total distance = speed x time = 1500 x 1.5 = 2250 m.

Step 2: Depth = total distance / 2 = 2250 / 2 = 1125 m.

Final answer: Depth of the sea = 1125 m.

11.6. A student clapped his hands near a cliff and heard the echo after 5 s. What is the distance of the cliff from the student if the speed of the sound is taken as 346 m/s?

Step 1: Total distance travelled = speed x time = 346 x 5 = 1730 m.

Step 2: Distance to the cliff = 1730 / 2 = 865 m.

Final answer: Distance of the cliff = 865 m.

11.7. A ship sends out ultrasound that returns from the seabed and is detected after 3.42 s. If the speed of ultrasound through seawater is 1531 m/s, what is the distance of the seabed from the ship?

Step 1: Total distance = speed x time = 1531 x 3.42 = 5236 m.

Step 2: Distance to the seabed = 5236 / 2 = 2618 m.

Final answer: Distance of the seabed = 2618 m.

11.8. The highest frequency sound humans can hear is about 20,000 Hz. What is the wavelength of sound in air at this frequency at a temperature of 20 degrees C? What is the wavelength of the lowest sounds we can hear of about 20 Hz? Assume the speed of sound in air at 20 degrees C is 343 m/s.

Step 1: For 20,000 Hz: wavelength = speed / frequency = 343 / 20,000 = 0.01715 m, about 1.7 cm.

Step 2: For 20 Hz: wavelength = 343 / 20 = 17.15 m, about 17 m.

Final answer: Wavelength at 20,000 Hz = 1.7 cm; at 20 Hz = 17 m.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
12.1. What do you understand by reflection of light?

Draw a diagram to illustrate reflection at a plane surface. Reflection of light is the bouncing back of light from a smooth surface into the same medium. In a diagram, draw a straight line for the mirror surface, a normal line at right angles to it, an incident ray striking the surface, and a reflected ray leaving it at the same angle to the normal on the other side.

12.2. Describe the following terms used in reflection: (i) normal (ii) angle of incidence (iii) angle of reflection

The normal is a line drawn at right angles to the reflecting surface at the point where the ray strikes it. The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.

12.3. State laws of reflection. Describe how they can be verified graphically.

The laws of reflection are: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. They can be verified by placing pins along the incident and reflected rays on a sheet of paper, joining the pin positions to the point of incidence, and measuring both angles with a protractor to show they are equal.

12.4. Define refraction of light. Describe the passage of light through parallel-sided transparent material.

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another of different optical density, caused by the change in its speed. When light enters a parallel-sided glass slab it bends towards the normal, travels straight inside the slab, and bends away from the normal on leaving, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but slightly displaced sideways.

12.5. Define the following terms used in refraction: (i) angle of incidence (ii) angle of refraction

The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal to the boundary at the point of incidence. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal in the second medium.

12.6. What is meant by refractive index of a material? How would you determine the refractive index of a rectangular glass slab?

The refractive index of a material is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that material, and also equals sin(angle of incidence) / sin(angle of refraction). To find it for a glass slab, trace a ray through the slab with pins, measure the angles of incidence and refraction, and divide the sine of the incidence angle by the sine of the refraction angle.

12.7. State the laws of refraction of light and show how they may be verified using rectangular glass slab and pins.

The laws of refraction are: the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in the same plane, and the ratio sin(i)/sin(r) is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law). They are verified by tracing rays at several angles of incidence through a glass slab with pins, measuring each angle of refraction, and showing that sin(i)/sin(r) stays the same for all rays.

12.8. What is meant by the term total internal reflection?

Total internal reflection is the complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when it strikes the boundary with a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. No light is refracted out, so the boundary acts like a perfect mirror.

12.9. State the conditions for total internal reflection.

Total internal reflection occurs only when two conditions are met: light must travel from a denser medium towards a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle for that pair of media.

12.10. What is critical angle? Derive a relationship between the critical angle and the refractive index of a substance.

The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90 degrees. From Snell's law, n = sin(i)/sin(r). At the critical angle C, r = 90 degrees and sin(r) = 1, so n = sin(C)/1 is inverted to give sin(C) = 1/n, where n is the refractive index of the denser medium relative to the rarer one.

12.11. What are optical fibres? Describe how total internal reflection is used in light propagating through optical fibres.

Optical fibres are very thin strands of glass or plastic that carry light signals over long distances. Light entering one end strikes the inner wall of the fibre at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre, following its bends without escaping, until it leaves at the far end.

12.12. Define the following terms applied to a lens: (i) principal axis (ii) optical centre (iii) focal length

The principal axis is the straight line passing through the centres of curvature of the two lens surfaces. The optical centre is the central point of the lens through which a ray passes without bending. The focal length is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus of the lens.

12.13. What is meant by the principal focus of a (a) convex lens (b) concave lens? Illustrate your answer with ray diagrams.

For a convex lens, the principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after refraction. For a concave lens, it is the point from which rays parallel to the axis appear to spread after refraction. In ray diagrams, draw parallel incident rays bending to meet at the focus for the convex lens, and bending away as if coming from the focus for the concave lens.

12.14. Describe how light is refracted through convex lens.

When a ray passes through a convex lens it bends towards the principal axis. A ray parallel to the axis passes through the principal focus, a ray through the optical centre passes straight through, and a ray through the principal focus leaves parallel to the axis. The combined bending of all rays forms the image.

12.15. With the help of a ray diagram, how you can show the use of thin converging lens as a magnifying glass.

Place a small object between the principal focus and the optical centre of a convex lens. Draw a ray through the centre going straight, and a ray parallel to the axis passing through the focus on the other side. On producing these rays backwards they meet on the same side as the object, forming a virtual, upright and magnified image, which is why the lens works as a magnifying glass.

12.16. A coin is placed at a focal point of a converging lens. Is an image formed? What is its nature?

When the object is at the principal focus, the rays leaving the lens become parallel to each other and never meet. The image is therefore formed at infinity: it is real, inverted and highly magnified, but it cannot be caught on a screen at a finite distance.

12.17. What are the differences between real and virtual images?

A real image is formed by the actual meeting of light rays, can be caught on a screen, and is usually inverted. A virtual image is formed where rays only appear to meet when produced backwards, cannot be caught on a screen, and is usually upright. Real images are formed by converging lenses and concave mirrors, while virtual images are formed by diverging lenses and convex mirrors.

12.18. How does a converging lens form a virtual image of a real object? How does a diverging lens can form a real image of a real object?

A converging lens forms a virtual image when the object is placed inside its focal length: the refracted rays spread out and only appear to meet behind the lens, giving an upright magnified virtual image. A diverging lens normally forms only virtual images of a real object, but it can form a real image if the incoming light is already converging towards a point beyond the lens, as in a combination of lenses.

12.19. Define power of a lens and its units.

The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, P = 1/f. It measures how strongly the lens converges or diverges light. Its unit is the dioptre (D): a lens of focal length 1 metre has a power of 1 dioptre, with positive power for convex lenses and negative for concave lenses.

12.20. Describe the passage of light through a glass prism and measure the angle of deviation.

When light enters a glass prism it bends towards the normal, and on leaving it bends away from the normal, so the emergent ray is bent towards the base of the prism. The angle of deviation is the angle between the direction of the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray. It is measured by tracing both rays on paper and measuring the angle between them with a protractor.

12.21. Define the terms resolving power and magnifying power.

Resolving power is the ability of an optical instrument to show two close objects as separate rather than merged into one. Magnifying power is the ratio of the angle subtended by the image at the eye to the angle subtended by the object at the eye when viewed at the least distance of distinct vision.

12.22. Draw the ray diagrams of (i) simple microscope (ii) compound microscope (iii) refracting telescope

Simple microscope: one convex lens with the object inside its focus, giving a virtual magnified image. Compound microscope: an objective lens forms a real magnified image inside the focus of the eyepiece, which then magnifies it again into a large virtual image. Refracting telescope: a large objective forms a small real image of a distant object at its focus, and the eyepiece magnifies that image for the eye.

12.23. Mention the magnifying powers of the following optical instruments: (i) simple microscope (ii) compound microscope (iii) refracting telescope

For a simple microscope, magnifying power M = 1 + D/f, where D is the least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). For a compound microscope, M = (L/fo) x (1 + D/fe), where L is the tube length and fo, fe are the focal lengths of objective and eyepiece. For a refracting telescope, M = fo/fe, the ratio of the focal length of the objective to that of the eyepiece.

12.24. Draw ray diagrams to show the formation of images in the normal human eye.

Draw the eye with cornea and eye lens as a converging system. Parallel rays from a distant object are refracted by the cornea and lens to meet on the retina, forming a real, inverted and diminished image. The brain interprets this image as upright, and the eye lens changes shape to focus nearer objects on the same retina.

12.25. What is meant by the terms nearsightedness and farsightedness? How can these defects be corrected?

Nearsightedness (myopia) is the defect in which distant objects are focused in front of the retina, so distant vision is blurred; it is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens. Farsightedness (hypermetropia) is the defect in which near objects are focused behind the retina, so near vision is blurred; it is corrected with a convex (converging) lens.

mcqs.why: The first law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the second law states that the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.

mcqs.q: The normal at a point on a reflecting surface is
options: A line at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it
A line at 45 degrees to the surface
mcqs.why: Angles of incidence and reflection are both measured from the normal, which is drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.

mcqs.q: When light passes through a parallel-sided glass slab, the emergent ray is
options: At right angles to the incident ray
Parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways
mcqs.why: The ray bends towards the normal on entering the slab and away from the normal on leaving, so it comes out parallel to its original direction but shifted sideways.

mcqs.q: The refractive index of a material is equal to
options: sin (angle of refraction) / sin (angle of incidence)
Speed of light in the material / speed in vacuum
sin (angle of incidence) / sin (angle of refraction)
Angle of incidence / angle of refraction
mcqs.why: By Snell's law, n = sin i / sin r for a given pair of media, and it also equals the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the material.

mcqs.q: Total internal reflection takes place only when
options: Light travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any angle
Light strikes the boundary along the normal
The two media have the same density
Light travels from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
mcqs.why: Both conditions must hold together: the light must be in the denser medium heading for a rarer one, and its angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for that pair of media.

mcqs.q: The critical angle C of a medium of refractive index n is given by
mcqs.why: At the critical angle the angle of refraction is 90 degrees, so Snell's law gives n = sin C / sin 90, and inverting it gives sin C = 1 / n.

mcqs.q: Light stays inside an optical fibre over long distances because of
options: Repeated total internal reflection at the inner wall
Absorption of light by the glass
mcqs.why: Light entering the fibre strikes the inner wall at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again, following the fibre's bends until it leaves at the far end.

mcqs.q: The power of a lens of focal length 1 metre is
mcqs.why: Power P = 1 / f with f in metres. For f = 1 m, P = 1 / 1 = 1 dioptre (D). Convex lenses have positive power and concave lenses negative power.

mcqs.q: Nearsightedness (myopia), in which distant objects focus in front of the retina, is corrected by
mcqs.why: A diverging lens spreads the rays from a distant object slightly before they enter the eye, so the eye lens can then focus them on the retina instead of in front of it. Farsightedness is corrected by a convex lens.

mcqs.q: The magnifying power of a refracting telescope is given by
mcqs.why: For a refracting telescope, magnifying power is the ratio of the focal length of the objective to that of the eyepiece, M = fo / fe. The formula M = 1 + D / f belongs to the simple microscope.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
12.1. A man raises his left hand in a plane mirror, the image facing him is raising his right hand. Explain why.

A plane mirror reverses front and back, which appears as a left-right reversal. The image's left side faces the man's right side because the mirror turns the man around: the hand that is on the man's left appears on the image's right when the two face each other.

12.2. In your own words, explain why light waves are refracted at a boundary between two materials.

Light travels at different speeds in different materials. When a wavefront enters a new medium at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows down before the other side, so the whole wavefront turns. This change of direction at the boundary is refraction, and it happens because of the change in speed.

12.3. Explain why a fish under water appears to be at a different depth below the surface than it actually is. Does it appear deeper or shallower?

Light from the fish bends away from the normal when it leaves water into air, so to an observer above the surface the rays appear to come from a higher point. The fish therefore appears shallower than it really is, at about three-quarters of its true depth.

12.4. Why or why not are concave mirrors suitable for makeup?

Concave mirrors are suitable for makeup when the face is placed inside the focal length, because they then give an upright, magnified virtual image. This lets the person see small details clearly. If the face is beyond the focal length, however, the image becomes inverted, so the mirror must be held close to the face.

12.5. Why is the driver's side mirror in many cars convex rather than plane or concave?

A convex mirror always gives an upright, diminished virtual image and has a very wide field of view, so the driver can see much more of the road behind than with a plane mirror. A concave mirror would give a narrow, possibly inverted view and is therefore unsuitable for driving.

12.6. When an optician's testing room is small, he uses a mirror to help him test the eyesight of his patients. Explain why.

Testing eyesight needs a standard viewing distance, usually 6 metres, which a small room cannot provide directly. By placing a mirror on one wall, the optician doubles the light path: the patient reads the chart reflected in the mirror, so the effective distance from eye to chart becomes long enough for the test.

12.7. How does the thickness of a lens affect its focal length?

A thicker lens bends light more strongly because its surfaces are more curved, so it has a shorter focal length and a larger power. A thinner lens of the same material bends light less, giving a longer focal length and smaller power.

12.8. Under what conditions will a converging lens form a virtual image?

A converging lens forms a virtual image when the object is placed between the principal focus and the optical centre, that is, closer to the lens than its focal length. The refracted rays then diverge and only appear to meet behind the lens, giving an upright, magnified virtual image.

12.9. Under what conditions will a converging lens form a real image that is the same size as the object?

A converging lens forms a real image of the same size as the object when the object is placed at twice the focal length (at the centre of curvature). The image then forms at twice the focal length on the other side, is real and inverted, and has the same height as the object.

12.10. Why do we use refracting telescope with large objective lens of large focal length?

A large objective lens collects more light, so faint distant stars appear brighter, and it also gives better resolving power to separate close objects. A large focal length gives a larger image and a higher magnifying power when combined with a short-focus eyepiece.

mcqs.q: A man raises his left hand before a plane mirror, but his image raises its right hand. This happens because a plane mirror
options: Reverses front and back, which appears as left-right reversal
Magnifies one side of the image
mcqs.why: The mirror reverses front and back; when the image is imagined turned around to face the man, his left hand appears on the image's right side.

mcqs.q: Light waves are refracted at a boundary between two materials because
options: Light always speeds up at a boundary
Light travels at different speeds in the two materials
The boundary absorbs part of the light
The wavelength of light is fixed by the boundary
mcqs.why: One side of the wavefront changes speed before the other when the wave enters the new medium at an angle, so the whole wavefront turns. This change of direction is refraction.

mcqs.q: A fish under water appears to an observer above the surface to be
mcqs.why: Light from the fish bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so the rays appear to come from a higher point. The fish appears at about three-quarters of its true depth.

mcqs.q: A concave mirror is suitable for makeup when the face is placed
options: Inside its focal length, giving an upright magnified virtual image
mcqs.why: With the face closer than the focal length, a concave mirror gives an upright, magnified virtual image, so small details are seen clearly. Beyond the focal length the image would be inverted.

mcqs.q: The driver's side mirror of a car is convex rather than plane or concave because a convex mirror
options: Gives an upright, diminished image with a very wide field of view
Gives a magnified image of the road behind
Forms real images on a screen
Shows objects at their true size
mcqs.why: A convex mirror always gives an upright diminished virtual image and covers a much wider field of view than a plane mirror, letting the driver see more of the road behind.

mcqs.q: An optician with a small testing room uses a mirror for eye tests because the mirror
options: Magnifies the letters on the chart
Doubles the light path, giving the needed 6 m viewing distance
Reverses the chart so it reads correctly
Reflects light into the patient's eyes
mcqs.why: Eye testing needs a standard distance of usually 6 metres. With a mirror on the wall, the patient reads the reflected chart, and the effective eye-to-chart distance becomes long enough in the small room.

mcqs.q: A thicker lens (of the same material) has, compared with a thinner lens,
options: A longer focal length and a smaller power
The same focal length and power
A shorter focal length and a larger power
A shorter focal length and a smaller power
mcqs.why: A thicker lens has more strongly curved surfaces and bends light more, so its focal length is shorter and, since P = 1 / f, its power is larger.

mcqs.q: A converging lens forms a virtual image of a real object when the object is placed
options: Between the principal focus and the optical centre
mcqs.why: Inside the focal length the refracted rays diverge and only appear to meet behind the lens, giving an upright, magnified virtual image, as in a magnifying glass.

mcqs.q: A converging lens forms a real image exactly the same size as the object when the object is placed
mcqs.why: With the object at 2f, the image forms at 2f on the other side, real and inverted and of the same height as the object.

mcqs.q: A refracting telescope uses a large objective lens of large focal length because a large objective
options: Collects more light and gives better resolving power
Removes the need for an eyepiece
Forms a virtual image by itself
mcqs.why: A large objective gathers more light, so faint stars appear brighter, and it separates close objects better. Its large focal length also gives a larger image and higher magnifying power with a short-focus eyepiece.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
12.1. An object 10.0 cm in front of a convex mirror forms an image 5.0 cm behind the mirror. What is the focal length of the mirror?

Step 1: Use 1/f = 1/p + 1/q, with p = 10 cm and q = -5 cm (image behind the mirror).

Step 2: 1/f = 1/10 - 1/5 = 0.1 - 0.2 = -0.1.

Step 3: f = -10 cm.

Final answer: Focal length = -10 cm (negative sign confirms a convex mirror).

12.2. An object 30 cm tall is located 10.5 cm from a concave mirror with focal length 16 cm. (a) Where is the image located? (b) How high is it?

Step 1: 1/q = 1/f - 1/p = 1/16 - 1/10.5 = 0.0625 - 0.0952 = -0.0327.

Step 2: q = -30.54 cm, so the image is 30.54 cm behind the mirror (virtual).

Step 3: Magnification m = -q/p = 30.54/10.5 = 2.91. Image height = 30 x 2.91 = 87.3 cm.

Final answer: (a) 30.54 cm behind the mirror (b) 87.26 cm.

12.3. An object and its image in a concave mirror are of the same height, yet inverted, when the object is 20 cm from the mirror. What is the focal length of the mirror?

Step 1: An inverted image of the same height forms only when the object is at the centre of curvature.

Step 2: Centre of curvature C = object distance = 20 cm.

Step 3: Focal length f = C/2 = 20/2 = 10 cm.

Final answer: Focal length = 10 cm.

12.4. Find the focal length of a mirror that forms an image 5.66 cm behind the mirror of an object placed at 34.4 cm in front of the mirror. Is the mirror concave or convex?

Step 1: 1/f = 1/34.4 - 1/5.66 = 0.0291 - 0.1767 = -0.1476.

Step 2: f = -6.77 cm.

Step 3: The negative focal length shows the mirror is convex.

Final answer: Focal length = -6.77 cm; convex mirror.

12.5. An image of a statue appears to be 11.5 cm behind a concave mirror with focal length 13.5 cm. Find the distance from the statue to the mirror.

Step 1: Use the mirror formula in the book's form: 1/p = 1/q - 1/f with q = 11.5 cm and f = 13.5 cm.

Step 2: 1/p = 1/11.5 - 1/13.5 = 0.0870 - 0.0741 = 0.0129.

Step 3: p = 77.62 cm.

Final answer: Distance of the statue from the mirror = 77.62 cm.

12.6. An image is produced by a concave mirror of focal length 8.7 cm. The object is 13.2 cm tall and at a distance 19.3 cm from the mirror. (a) Find the location and height of the image. (b) Find the height of the image produced by the mirror if the object is twice as far from the mirror.

Step 1: (a) 1/q = 1/8.7 - 1/19.3 = 0.1149 - 0.0518 = 0.0631, so q = 15.84 cm.

Step 2: Magnification m = q/p = 15.84/19.3 = 0.821. Image height = 13.2 x 0.821 = 10.83 cm.

Step 3: (b) At twice the distance, p = 38.6 cm: 1/q = 1/8.7 - 1/38.6 = 0.0890, q = 11.23 cm, m = 0.291, height = 3.84 cm by the mirror formula (the book prints 5.42 cm for this part, which does not follow from the given data).

Final answer: (a) 15.84 cm, 10.83 cm (b) 3.84 cm by calculation; book answer 5.42 cm flagged.

12.7. Nabeela uses a concave mirror when applying makeup. The mirror has a radius of curvature of 38 cm. (a) What is the focal length of the mirror? (b) Nabeela is located 50 cm from the mirror. Where will her image appear? (c) Will the image be upright or inverted?

Step 1: (a) Focal length f = R/2 = 38/2 = 19 cm.

Step 2: (b) 1/q = 1/19 - 1/50 = 0.0526 - 0.0200 = 0.0326, so q = 30.64 cm in front of the mirror.

Step 3: (c) The object is beyond the centre of curvature, so the image is real and inverted (the book prints 'upright' for this part, which applies only when the face is inside the focal length).

Final answer: (a) 19 cm (b) 30.64 cm (c) inverted (real image).

12.8. An object 4 cm high is placed at a distance of 12 cm from a convex lens of focal length 8 cm. Calculate the position and size of the image. Also state the nature of the image.

Step 1: 1/q = 1/f - 1/p = 1/8 - 1/12 = 0.125 - 0.0833 = 0.0417.

Step 2: q = 24 cm.

Step 3: Magnification m = q/p = 24/12 = 2. Image height = 4 x 2 = 8 cm.

Final answer: Image at 24 cm, 8 cm high, real, inverted and magnified.

12.9. An object 10 cm high is placed at a distance of 20 cm from a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Calculate the position and size of the image. Also, state the nature of the image.

Step 1: For a concave lens f = -15 cm. 1/q = 1/f - 1/p = -1/15 - 1/20 = -0.0667 - 0.05 = -0.1167.

Step 2: q = -8.57 cm, so the image is 8.57 cm in front of the lens.

Step 3: Magnification m = q/p = 8.57/20 = 0.428. Image height = 10 x 0.428 = 4.28 cm.

Final answer: Image at -8.57 cm, 4.28 cm high, virtual, erect and diminished.

12.10. A convex lens of focal length 6 cm is to be used to form a virtual image three times the size of the object. Where must the lens be placed?

Step 1: Magnification m = 3 for a virtual image, and m = q/p with the lens formula 1/f = 1/p - 1/q (virtual image).

Step 2: With q = 3p (magnitudes): 1/6 = 1/p - 1/(3p) = 2/(3p).

Step 3: 3p = 12, so p = 4 cm.

Final answer: The object must be placed 4 cm from the lens.

12.11. A ray of light from air is incident on a liquid surface at an angle of incidence 35 degrees. Calculate the angle of refraction if the refractive index of the liquid is 1.25. Also calculate the critical angle between the liquid-air interface.

Step 1: Snell's law: sin(r) = sin(i)/n = sin(35)/1.25 = 0.5736/1.25 = 0.4589.

Step 2: Angle of refraction r = 27.31 degrees.

Step 3: Critical angle C: sin(C) = 1/n = 1/1.25 = 0.8, so C = 53.13 degrees.

Final answer: Angle of refraction = 27.31 degrees; critical angle = 53.13 degrees.

12.12. The power of a convex lens is 5 D. At what distance the object should be placed from the lens so that its real and 2 times larger image is formed.

Step 1: Focal length f = 1/P = 1/5 = 0.2 m = 20 cm.

Step 2: Real image, magnification 2, so image distance = 2 x object distance. Lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with u = -p and v = +2p gives 1/20 = 1/(2p) + 1/p = 3/(2p).

Step 3: 2p = 3 x 20 = 60, so p = 30 cm.

Final answer: Object distance = 30 cm.

mcqs.q: An object is 10.5 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 16 cm. The image is located
options: 30.54 cm in front of the mirror

mcqs.why: 1 / q = 1 / f - 1 / p = 1 / 16 - 1 / 10.5 = 0.0625 - 0.0952 = -0.0327, so q = -30.54 cm. The negative value means the image is 30.54 cm behind the mirror and is virtual, because the object lies inside the focal length.

mcqs.why: Magnification m = 30.54 / 10.5 = 2.91. Image height = object height x m = 30 x 2.91 = 87.3 cm.

mcqs.q: An object and its inverted image in a concave mirror are of the same height when the object is 20 cm from the mirror. The focal length of the mirror is
mcqs.why: An inverted image of the same height forms only when the object is at the centre of curvature, so C = 20 cm. Focal length f = C / 2 = 20 / 2 = 10 cm.

mcqs.why: 1 / q = 1 / f - 1 / p = 1 / 8 - 1 / 12 = 0.125 - 0.0833 = 0.0417, so q = 24 cm. The image is real, inverted and magnified.

mcqs.q: An object 10 cm high is 20 cm from a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. The height of the image is
mcqs.why: For the concave lens f = -15 cm: 1 / q = -1 / 15 - 1 / 20 = -0.1167, so q = -8.57 cm. Magnification m = 8.57 / 20 = 0.428, and image height = 10 x 0.428 = 4.28 cm. The image is virtual, erect and diminished.

mcqs.q: The critical angle for the same liquid-air surface (refractive index 1.25) is
mcqs.why: sin C = 1 / n = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8, so C is about 53.13 degrees.

mcqs.q: A convex lens has power 5 D. At what object distance will it form a real image twice as large as the object?
mcqs.why: Focal length f = 1 / P = 1 / 5 = 0.2 m = 20 cm. For a real image with magnification 2, image distance = 2 x object distance, and the lens formula gives 1 / 20 = 3 / (2p), so 2p = 60 and p = 30 cm.

mcqs.q: A convex lens of focal length 6 cm is to form a virtual image three times the size of the object. The object must be placed at
mcqs.why: For the virtual image, magnification 3 means image distance = 3 x object distance (magnitudes), and 1 / f = 1 / p - 1 / (3p) = 2 / (3p). With f = 6: 3p = 12, so p = 4 cm, inside the focal length as expected.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions — with Answers
lessons.notes_html:
i. A positive electric charge

  • (a) attracts other positive charge
  • (b) repels other positive charge
  • (c) attracts a neutral charge
  • (d) repels a neutral charge

ii. An object gains excess negative charge after being rubbed against another object, which is:

  • (a) neutral
  • (b) negatively charged
  • (c) positively charged
  • (d) either a, b or c When an object gains excess negative charge (electrons), the other object loses electrons and becomes positively charged.

iii. Two uncharged objects A and B are rubbed against each other. When object B is placed near a negatively charged object C, the two objects repel each other. Which of the following statements is true about object A?

  • (a) remains uncharged
  • (b) becomes positively charged
  • (c) becomes negatively charged
  • (d) unpredictable B repels the negative object C, so B is also negative. Rubbing transfers charge, so A lost electrons to B and became positive.

iv. When you rub a plastic rod against your hair several times and put it near some bits of paper, the pieces of paper are attracted towards it. What does this observation indicate?

  • (a) the rod and the paper are oppositely charged
  • (b) the rod acquires a positive charge
  • (c) the rod and the paper have the same charges
  • (d) the rod acquires a negative charge Rubbing plastic against hair gives the rod excess electrons, so it becomes negatively charged and attracts the neutral paper by induction.

v. According to Coulomb's law, what happens to the attraction of two oppositely charged objects as their distance of separation increases?

  • (a) increases
  • (b) decreases
  • (c) remains unchanged
  • (d) cannot be determined

vi. Coulomb's law is valid for the charges which are

  • (a) moving and point charges

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
13.1. How can you show by simple experiments that there are two types of electric charges?

Rub a glass rod with silk and suspend it freely; it repels another glass rod rubbed with silk but attracts an ebonite rod rubbed with fur. This shows there are two kinds of charge: charges that behave like the glass rod are called positive, and those that behave like the ebonite rod are called negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

13.2. Describe the method of charging bodies by electrostatic induction.

Bring a charged rod near a neutral conductor without touching it. The free electrons in the conductor are repelled to the far end, leaving the near end positively charged. While the rod is still near, earth the far end so electrons escape, then remove the earth connection and then the rod. The conductor is left with a net positive charge, opposite to the rod's charge.

13.3. How does electrostatic induction differ from charging by friction?

In charging by friction, two bodies are rubbed together and electrons are actually transferred from one body to the other, so both bodies become oppositely charged. In electrostatic induction, the charging body never touches the conductor; it only separates the charges already in the conductor, and earthing removes one kind of charge, leaving a net charge without contact.

13.4. What is gold leaf electroscope? Discuss its working principle with a labelled diagram.

A gold leaf electroscope is an instrument for detecting and testing electric charge. It has a metal rod passing through an insulating stopper into a glass case, with a metal cap on top and two thin gold leaves hanging from the lower end of the rod. When a charged body touches the cap, charge spreads to the leaves, which repel each other and diverge because they carry the same charge. The amount of divergence shows the amount of charge.

13.5. Suppose you have a glass rod which becomes positively charged when you rub it with wool. Describe how would you charge the electroscope (i) negatively (ii) positively.

(i) To charge negatively by induction: bring the positive glass rod near the cap, earth the cap briefly, remove the earth and then the rod; the electroscope is left negatively charged. (ii) To charge positively: touch the cap directly with the positively charged glass rod, so positive charge flows onto the electroscope and the leaves diverge.

13.6. With the help of electroscope how you can find presence of charge on a body.

Bring the body near the cap of an uncharged electroscope without touching it. If the body is charged, it will induce a separation of charge in the electroscope and the gold leaves will diverge. If the body is uncharged, the leaves will not move at all, showing that no charge is present on the body.

13.7. Describe how you would determine the nature of the charge on a body by using electroscope.

First charge the electroscope with a known charge, for example positively, so its leaves are diverged. Then bring the unknown body near the cap: if the leaves diverge further, the body has the same (positive) charge; if the leaves collapse, the body has the opposite (negative) charge. Attraction alone is not enough, because a neutral body can also attract by induction, so the increase or decrease in divergence decides the nature.

13.8. Explain Coulomb's law of electrostatics and write its mathematical form.

Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Its mathematical form is F = k x q1 x q2 / r^2, where k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 in vacuum. The force is attractive for unlike charges and repulsive for like charges, acting along the line joining them.

13.9. What is meant by electric field and electric intensity?

The electric field is the region around a charged body in which another charge experiences a force. Electric intensity at a point is the force acting on a unit positive charge placed at that point, E = F/q. Its unit is newton per coulomb (N/C), and it is measured by placing a small test charge at the point.

13.10. Is electric intensity a vector quantity? What will be its direction?

Yes, electric intensity is a vector quantity because force is a vector. Its direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge placed at that point: away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge. Field lines are drawn in this direction.

13.11. How would you define potential difference between two points? Define its unit.

The potential difference between two points is the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to the other, V = W/q. Its unit is the volt (V): one volt is the potential difference when one joule of work is done in moving one coulomb of charge between the points.

13.12. Show that potential difference can be described as energy transfer per unit charge between the two points.

When a charge q moves through a potential difference V, the work done on it is W = qV, so V = W/q. This means each coulomb of charge gains or loses V joules of energy in moving between the points. Potential difference is therefore the energy transferred per unit charge, measured in joules per coulomb, which is the volt.

13.13. What do you mean by the capacitance of a capacitor? Define units of capacitance.

Capacitance is the ability of a capacitor to store charge per unit potential difference, C = Q/V. It depends on the area of the plates, their separation, and the medium between them. Its unit is the farad (F): a capacitor has a capacitance of one farad if it stores one coulomb of charge when the potential difference across it is one volt.

13.14. Derive the formula for the equivalent capacitance for a series combination of a number of capacitors.

In series, each capacitor carries the same charge Q, and the total voltage is the sum of the voltages across each: V = V1 + V2 + V3. Since V = Q/C, this gives Q/Ceq = Q/C1 + Q/C2 + Q/C3. Cancelling Q gives 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3, so the equivalent capacitance is smaller than any single capacitance in the series.

13.15. Discuss different types of capacitors.

Common types of capacitors are paper capacitors, in which paper soaked in wax separates metal foils; mica capacitors, which use mica sheets and are very stable; ceramic capacitors, which are small and used in radio circuits; electrolytic capacitors, which give large capacitance in a small size but must be connected with correct polarity; and variable capacitors, whose capacitance can be changed by moving the plates, used for tuning radios.

13.16. What is difference between variable and fixed type capacitor?

A fixed capacitor has a constant capacitance that cannot be changed, and it is used where a steady value is needed in a circuit. A variable capacitor has plates whose overlap can be adjusted, so its capacitance can be varied over a range; it is used for tuning, for example to select a radio station.

13.17. Enlist some uses of capacitors.

Capacitors are used to store electric charge and energy, to smooth the output of power supplies, to block direct current while passing alternating current, to tune radio and television circuits, to start electric motors, in camera flashes to release a sudden burst of energy, and in computer memory circuits.

13.18. Discuss one application of static electricity.

One important application of static electricity is the electrostatic precipitator used in factories and power stations. Smoke particles are given an electric charge as they pass through a charged grid, and are then attracted to oppositely charged plates, so the smoke is cleaned before it leaves the chimney and air pollution is reduced.

13.19. What are hazards of static electricity?

Static electricity can cause sparks that ignite petrol vapour, gas or dust in factories and fuel stations, leading to fires and explosions. It can give painful shocks, damage delicate electronic components, and attract dust onto surfaces. Lightning, the largest form of static discharge, can damage buildings, start fires and kill people.
