lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
13.1. An electrified rod attracts pieces of paper. After a while these pieces fly away! Why?

At first the charged rod attracts the neutral paper by induction, because the near side of each piece acquires opposite charge. After contact, each piece gains the same charge as the rod, so it is then repelled and flies away. The pieces therefore first stick to the rod and then jump off it.

13.2. How much negative charge has been removed from a positively charged electroscope, if it has a charge of 7.5 x 10^-11 C?

A positively charged electroscope has a deficiency of electrons, so its positive charge equals the charge of the electrons removed. Removing electrons of total charge 7.5 x 10^-11 C leaves the electroscope with a net positive charge of 7.5 x 10^-11 C, since each electron carries 1.6 x 10^-19 C and about 4.7 x 10^8 electrons have been removed.

13.3. In what direction will a positively charged particle move in an electric field?

A positively charged particle moves in the direction of the electric field, that is, along the field lines away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge. This is because the electric force on a positive charge acts in the same direction as the field intensity.

13.4. Does each capacitor carry equal charge in series combination? Explain.

Yes, in a series combination each capacitor carries the same charge. When the combination is connected to a battery, the battery moves charge onto the first plate, which induces an equal and opposite charge on the second plate, and this induction continues through the whole chain. Every capacitor therefore ends up with the same magnitude of charge, although their voltages differ.

13.5. Each capacitor in parallel combination has equal potential difference between its two plates. Justify the statement.

In a parallel combination, one plate of every capacitor is connected directly to one terminal of the battery and the other plate to the other terminal. All the capacitors are therefore connected across the same two points, so each one experiences the full battery voltage. Hence the potential difference across each capacitor is the same, while their charges differ according to their capacitances.

13.6. Perhaps you have seen a gasoline truck trailing a metal chain beneath it. What purpose does the chain serve?

As a gasoline truck moves, friction can build up static charge on its body. The trailing metal chain touches the ground continuously and conducts this charge safely to the earth, preventing a spark. Without the chain, a spark could ignite the petrol vapour and cause a fire or explosion.

13.7. If a high-voltage power line fell across your car while you were in the car, why should you not come out of the car?

The metal body of the car acts like a cage: the charge stays on the outside of the car and the inside remains safe. If you step out while touching the car and the ground at the same time, the current can pass through your body to the earth and electrocute you. You should stay inside until the power is switched off and help arrives.

13.8. Explain why a glass rod can be charged by rubbing when held by hand but an iron rod cannot be charged by rubbing, if held by hand?

Glass is an insulator, so the charge produced by rubbing stays where it is formed on the rod. Iron is a conductor, so any charge produced flows at once through the hand and body to the earth, leaving the rod uncharged. An iron rod can be charged by rubbing only if it is held by an insulating handle.

mcqs.why: Number of electrons = total charge removed / charge per electron = (7.5 x 10^-11) / (1.6 x 10^-19), which is about 4.7 x 10^8 electrons.

mcqs.why: Friction during travel can charge the truck's body. The trailing chain touches the ground continuously and leaks this charge to earth; without it, a spark could ignite the petrol vapour.

options: The metal body acts like a cage, keeping the charge on the outside and the inside safe
The inside of the car has no electric charge anywhere near it

mcqs.why: Charge stays on the outer surface of the metal body, so the interior remains safe. Stepping out while touching both car and ground would let current pass through the body to earth.

mcqs.why: Charge made by rubbing stays on an insulator like glass. On a conductor like iron it flows away at once through the hand and body to earth, unless the rod is held by an insulating handle.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
13.1. The charge of how many negatively charged particles would be equal to 100 microC? Assume charge on one negative particle is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

Step 1: Total charge Q = 100 microC = 100 x 10^-6 C = 10^-4 C.

Step 2: Number of particles n = Q / e = 10^-4 / (1.6 x 10^-19).

Step 3: n = 6.25 x 10^14.

Final answer: 6.25 x 10^14 particles.

13.2. Two point charges q1 = 10 microC and q2 = 5 microC are placed at a distance of 150 cm. What will be the Coulomb's force between them? Also find the direction of the force.

Step 1: r = 150 cm = 1.5 m; q1 = 10 x 10^-6 C; q2 = 5 x 10^-6 C.

Step 2: F = k x q1 x q2 / r^2 = (9 x 10^9) x (10 x 10^-6) x (5 x 10^-6) / (1.5)^2.

Step 3: F = (9 x 10^9 x 50 x 10^-12) / 2.25 = 0.45 / 2.25 = 0.2 N.

Step 4: Both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive, acting away from each other.

Final answer: 0.2 N, repulsion.

13.3. The force of repulsion between two identical positive charges is 0.8 N, when the charges are 0.1 m apart. Find the value of each charge.

Step 1: F = k x q^2 / r^2, so q^2 = F x r^2 / k.

Step 2: q^2 = 0.8 x (0.1)^2 / (9 x 10^9) = 0.008 / (9 x 10^9) = 8.89 x 10^-13.

Step 3: q = square root (8.89 x 10^-13) = 9.4 x 10^-7 C.

Final answer: Each charge = 9.4 x 10^-7 C.

13.4. Two charges repel each other with a force of 0.1 N when they are 5 cm apart. Find the force between the same charges when they are 2 cm apart.

Step 1: Force is inversely proportional to distance squared: F2 / F1 = (r1 / r2)^2.

Step 2: F2 = 0.1 x (5/2)^2 = 0.1 x 6.25 = 0.625 N, about 0.62 N.

Final answer: Force = 0.62 N.

13.5. The electric potential at a point in an electric field is 10^4 V. If a charge of +100 microC is brought from infinity to this point, what would be the amount of work done on it?

Step 1: Work W = qV.

Step 2: q = 100 microC = 100 x 10^-6 C = 10^-4 C; V = 10^4 V.

Step 3: W = 10^-4 x 10^4 = 1 J.

Final answer: Work done = 1 J.

13.6. A point charge of +2 C is transferred from a point at potential 100 V to a point at potential 50 V. What would be the energy supplied by the charge?

Step 1: Potential difference = 100 - 50 = 50 V.

Step 2: Energy supplied = q x potential difference = 2 x 50 = 100 J.

Final answer: Energy supplied = 100 J.

13.7. A capacitor holds 0.06 coulombs of charge when fully charged by a 9 volt battery. Calculate capacitance of the capacitor.

Step 1: C = Q / V = 0.06 / 9.

Step 2: C = 0.00667 F = 6.67 x 10^-3 F.

Final answer: Capacitance = 6.67 x 10^-3 F.

13.8. A capacitor holds 0.03 coulombs of charge when fully charged by a 6 volt battery. How much voltage would be required for it to hold 2 coulombs of charge?

Step 1: Capacitance C = Q / V = 0.03 / 6 = 0.005 F.

Step 2: For Q = 2 C: V = Q / C = 2 / 0.005 = 400 V.

Final answer: Voltage required = 400 V.

13.9. Two capacitors of capacitances 6 microF and 12 microF are connected in series with 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance of the combination. Find the charge and the potential difference across each capacitor.

Step 1: 1/Ceq = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, so Ceq = 4 microF.

Step 2: Charge (same for both) Q = Ceq x V = 4 x 12 = 48 microC.

Step 3: Voltage across 6 microF = 48/6 = 8 V; across 12 microF = 48/12 = 4 V.

Final answer: Ceq = 4 microF, charge = 48 microC, voltages 8 V and 4 V.

13.10. Two capacitors of capacitances 6 microF and 12 microF are connected in parallel with a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance of the combination. Find the charge and the potential difference across each capacitor.

Step 1: Ceq = 6 + 12 = 18 microF.

Step 2: Voltage across each = 12 V (parallel).

Step 3: Charge on 6 microF = 6 x 12 = 72 microC; on 12 microF = 12 x 12 = 144 microC.

Final answer: Ceq = 18 microF, charges 72 microC and 144 microC, voltage 12 V each.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
14.1. Define and explain the term electric current.

Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, I = Q/t. In a metal wire it is the flow of free electrons, and it is measured in amperes: one ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point in one second.

14.2. What is the difference between electronic current and conventional current?

Electronic current is the actual flow of electrons, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of a source. Conventional current is the direction in which positive charge would flow, from positive to negative terminal, and it is the direction used in circuit diagrams. The two directions are opposite to each other.

14.3. What do we mean by the term e.m.f? Is it really a force? Explain.

E.m.f. (electromotive force) is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge, measured in volts. It is not really a force: the name is historical. A cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V supplies 1.5 joules of energy to each coulomb of charge passing through it.

14.4. How can we differentiate between e.m.f. and potential difference?

E.m.f. is the total energy supplied per unit charge by a source when no current flows, or the work done by the source. Potential difference is the energy used per unit charge between two points of a circuit when current flows. E.m.f. is measured across the source on open circuit, while potential difference is measured across a component in a working circuit and is less than the e.m.f. because some energy is lost in the internal resistance.

14.5. Explain Ohm's law. What are its limitations?

Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided its temperature and physical state remain constant: V = IR. Its limitations are that it holds only for ohmic conductors at constant temperature; it fails for diodes, transistors, filament lamps and electrolytes, whose resistance changes with current or voltage.

14.6. Define resistance and its units.

Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current, R = V/I. Its unit is the ohm (symbol ohm): a conductor has a resistance of one ohm if a potential difference of one volt across it produces a current of one ampere.

14.7. What is the difference between conductors and insulators?

Conductors are materials that allow electric charge to flow easily because they have many free electrons, for example copper, aluminium and iron. Insulators are materials that do not allow charge to flow easily because their electrons are tightly bound, for example rubber, plastic, wood and glass.

14.8. Explain the energy dissipation in a resistance. What is Joule's law?

When current flows through a resistance, the moving electrons collide with the atoms of the conductor and give up energy, which appears as heat. Joule's law states that the heat produced is H = I^2 x R x t, where I is current, R is resistance and t is time. This heating effect is used in heaters and bulbs but is a loss in power transmission.

14.9. What is difference between D.C and A.C?

Direct current (D.C.) flows always in one direction with a steady value, as supplied by cells and batteries. Alternating current (A.C.) repeatedly reverses direction and changes in magnitude, as supplied by generators and the mains. Household supply in Pakistan is 220 V A.C. at 50 Hz.

14.10. Discuss the main features of parallel combination of resistors.

In a parallel combination, each resistor is connected across the same voltage, so the voltage across each is equal. The total current divides among the branches in inverse proportion to their resistances. The equivalent resistance is given by 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., and it is smaller than the smallest single resistance in the combination.

14.11. Determine the equivalent resistance of series combination of resistors.

In series, the same current flows through every resistor and the total voltage is the sum of the voltages across each: V = V1 + V2 + V3. Since V = IR, this gives I x Req = I x R1 + I x R2 + I x R3. Cancelling I gives Req = R1 + R2 + R3, so the equivalent resistance is the sum of the separate resistances.

14.12. Describe briefly the hazards of household electricity.

Household electricity can cause electric shocks that may be fatal, fires from short circuits and overloaded wires, and burns from contact with live parts. Damaged insulation, wet hands, and faulty appliances increase the danger, and a short circuit can melt wires and set fire to nearby materials.

14.13. Describe four safety measures that should be taken in connection with the household circuit.

Four safety measures are: use fuses or circuit breakers that break the circuit on excess current; earth all metal appliances so a fault current flows safely to the ground; use insulated wires and switches and replace damaged ones at once; and never touch switches or appliances with wet hands, and keep water away from sockets.

14.14. Design a circuit diagram for a study room that needs the following equipments in parallel: (a) One 100 W lamp operated by one switch. (b) One reading lamp fitted with a 40 W bulb which can be switched ON and OFF from two points. (c) What is the advantage of connecting the equipments in parallel instead of series?

Draw the mains supply with a live and a neutral line. Connect the 100 W lamp in one branch with its own switch in series with it. Connect the 40 W reading lamp in a second branch with two two-way switches, one at each end of the room, wired so either switch can turn it on or off. (c) In parallel, each appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently, and if one fails the others keep working; in series they would share the voltage and all would go off together.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
14.1. Why in conductors is charge transferred by free electrons rather than by positive charges?

In a metal conductor the positive ions are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot move, while a large number of electrons are free to move through the lattice. When a voltage is applied, these free electrons drift towards the positive terminal, so charge is carried by electrons and not by the fixed positive ions.

14.2. What is the difference between a cell and a battery?

A cell is a single unit that converts chemical energy into electrical energy, for example a 1.5 V dry cell. A battery is a combination of two or more cells connected together, usually in series, to give a larger voltage, for example a 12 V car battery made of six 2 V cells.

14.3. Can current flow in a circuit without potential difference?

No, a steady current cannot flow without a potential difference. Current is the flow of charge driven by an electric field, which exists only when there is a potential difference between two points. Without it, the free electrons move randomly but there is no net flow in any direction.

14.4. Two points on an object are at different electric potentials. Does charge necessarily flow between them?

Not necessarily. Charge flows only if there is a conducting path between the points. If the points are separated by an insulator, no charge can flow even though a potential difference exists, just as a charged capacitor holds its charge until a conducting path is provided.

14.5. In order to measure current in a circuit why is an ammeter always connected in series?

An ammeter measures the current passing through it, so it must be placed in the path of the current, that is, in series with the component. It has a very low resistance so it does not change the circuit current appreciably. Connected in parallel it would short-circuit the component and be damaged by the large current.

14.6. In order to measure voltage in a circuit why is a voltmeter always connected in parallel? Discuss.

A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points, so it must be connected across the component, that is, in parallel with it. It has a very high resistance so it draws almost no current and does not disturb the circuit. Connected in series it would block the current and give a wrong reading.

14.7. How many watt-hours are there in 1000 joules?

One watt-hour is the energy used by one watt for one hour: 1 Wh = 1 W x 3600 s = 3600 J. Therefore 1000 J = 1000/3600 Wh = 0.278 Wh, about 0.28 watt-hours.

14.8. From your experience in watching cars on the roads at night, are automobile headlamps connected in series or in parallel?

Headlamps are connected in parallel. This is clear because when one headlamp fails, the other keeps shining, and both shine with full brightness. In series, one failure would switch off both lamps and each would get only half the voltage.

14.9. A certain flash-light can use a 10 ohm bulb or a 5 ohm bulb. Which bulb should be used to get the brighter light? Which bulb will discharge the battery first?

The 5 ohm bulb should be used for brighter light, because at the same battery voltage it draws more current (I = V/R) and uses more power (P = V^2/R). For the same reason, the 5 ohm bulb will discharge the battery first, since it consumes energy faster.

14.10. It is impracticable to connect an electric bulb and an electric heater in series. Why?

A bulb and a heater need very different currents and voltages: the heater draws a large current while the bulb needs a small one. In series the same current must flow through both, so neither would work at its rated value, the bulb would be dim or could burn out, and switching off one would switch off the other.

14.11. Does a fuse in a circuit control the potential difference or the current?

A fuse controls the current. It is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds its safe rating, protecting the wiring and appliances. It does not control the potential difference, which is fixed by the supply.

mcqs.why: The positive ions of a metal cannot move from their lattice positions. When a voltage is applied, the free electrons drift towards the positive terminal and carry the charge.

mcqs.why: Without a potential difference the free electrons move randomly with no net flow in any direction. A potential difference provides the field that drives a steady current.

options: The points are at the same temperature

Its low resistance would short the component

mcqs.why: A voltmeter is connected across the component whose potential difference is needed. Its high resistance means it barely disturbs the circuit; in series it would block the current and read wrongly.

mcqs.why: One watt-hour = 1 W x 3600 s = 3600 J. So 1000 J = 1000 / 3600 Wh, which is about 0.278 Wh, about 0.28 Wh.

The current, by melting and breaking the circuit when the current exceeds its rating
mcqs.why: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when the current exceeds its safe rating, protecting the wiring and appliances. It does not control the potential difference, which is fixed by the supply.

lessons.notes_html:
14.1. A current of 3 mA is flowing through a wire for 1 minute. What is the charge flowing through the wire?

Step 1: Q = I x t. I = 3 mA = 3 x 10^-3 A; t = 1 minute = 60 s.

Step 2: Q = 3 x 10^-3 x 60 = 180 x 10^-3 C = 0.18 C.

Final answer: Charge = 180 x 10^-3 C.

14.2. At 100,000 ohm, how much current flows through your body if you touch the terminals of a 12 V battery? If your skin is wet, so that your resistance is only 1000 ohm, how much current would you receive from the same battery?

Step 1: I = V/R = 12 / 100,000 = 1.2 x 10^-4 A (dry skin).

Step 2: I = 12 / 1000 = 1.2 x 10^-2 A (wet skin).

Final answer: 1.2 x 10^-4 A dry; 1.2 x 10^-2 A wet.

14.3. The resistance of a conductor wire is 10 megaohm.

If a potential difference of 100 volts is applied across its ends, then find the value of current passing through it in mA.

Step 1: R = 10 megaohm = 10 x 10^6 ohm; V = 100 V.

Step 2: I = V/R = 100 / (10 x 10^6) = 10 x 10^-6 A = 0.01 mA.

Final answer: Current = 0.01 mA.

14.4. By applying a potential difference of 10 V across a conductor, a current of 1.5 A passes through it. How much energy would be obtained from the current in 2 minutes?

Step 1: Energy E = V x I x t. t = 2 minutes = 120 s.

Step 2: E = 10 x 1.5 x 120 = 1800 J.

Final answer: Energy = 1800 J.

14.5. Two resistances of 2 kilo-ohm and 8 kilo-ohm are joined in series, if a 10 V battery is connected across the ends of this combination, find: (a) The equivalent resistance of the series combination. (b) Current passing through each of the resistances. (c) The potential difference across each resistance.

Step 1: (a) Req = 2 + 8 = 10 kilo-ohm.

Step 2: (b) Current I = V/Req = 10 / 10,000 = 0.001 A = 1 mA, the same through both.

Step 3: (c) V across 2 kilo-ohm = 0.001 x 2000 = 2 V; across 8 kilo-ohm = 0.001 x 8000 = 8 V.

Final answer: (a) 10 kilo-ohm (b) 1 mA (c) 2 V, 8 V.

14.6. Two resistances of 6 kilo-ohm and 12 kilo-ohm are connected in parallel. A 6 V battery is connected across its ends, find: (a) Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination. (b) Current passing through each of the resistances. (c) Potential difference across each of the resistance.

Step 1: (a) 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, so Req = 4 kilo-ohm.

Step 2: (b) Current through 6 kilo-ohm = 6/6000 = 1 mA; through 12 kilo-ohm = 6/12000 = 0.5 mA.

Step 3: (c) In parallel, each resistor gets the full battery voltage = 6 V.

Final answer: (a) 4 kilo-ohm (b) 1 mA, 0.5 mA (c) 6 V.

14.7. An electric bulb is marked with 220 V, 100 W. Find the resistance of the filament of the bulb. If the bulb is used 5 hours daily, find the energy in kilowatt-hour consumed by the bulb in one month (30 days).

Step 1: Resistance R = V^2 / P = (220)^2 / 100 = 48,400 / 100 = 484 ohm.

Step 2: Energy per day = 100 W x 5 h = 500 Wh = 0.5 kWh.

Step 3: Energy in 30 days = 0.5 x 30 = 15 kWh.

Final answer: Resistance = 484 ohm; energy = 15 kWh.

14.8. An incandescent light bulb with an operating resistance of 95 ohm is labelled '150 W.' Is this bulb designed for use in a 120 V circuit or a 220 V circuit?

Step 1: Power P = V^2 / R, so V = square root (P x R) = square root (150 x 95) = square root (14,250).

Step 2: V = 119.4 V, about 120 V.

Final answer: The bulb is designed for a 120 V circuit.

14.9. A house is installed with (a) 10 bulbs of 60 W each used 5 hours daily. (b) 4 fans of 75 W each run 10 hours daily. (c) One T.V. of 100 W used 5 hours daily. (d) One electric iron of 1000 W used 2 hours daily. If the cost of one unit of electricity is Rs. 4, find the monthly expenditure of electricity (one month = 30 days).

Step 1: Bulbs: 10 x 60 x 5 = 3000 Wh/day. Fans: 4 x 75 x 10 = 3000 Wh/day.

Step 2: T.V.: 100 x 5 = 500 Wh/day. Iron: 1000 x 2 = 2000 Wh/day.

Step 3: Total per day = 3000 + 3000 + 500 + 2000 = 8500 Wh = 8.5 kWh (units).

Step 4: Monthly units = 8.5 x 30 = 255 units. Cost = 255 x 4 = Rs. 1020.

Final answer: Monthly expenditure = Rs. 1020.

14.10. A 100 W lamp bulb and a 4 kW water heater are connected to a 250 V supply. Calculate (a) the current which flows in each appliance (b) the resistance of each appliance when in use.

Step 1: (a) Lamp current = P/V = 100/250 = 0.4 A. Heater current = 4000/250 = 16 A.

Step 2: (b) Lamp resistance = V/I = 250/0.4 = 625 ohm. Heater resistance = 250/16 = 15.62 ohm.

Final answer: (a) 0.4 A, 16 A (b) 625 ohm, 15.62 ohm.

14.11. A resistor of resistance 5.6 ohm is connected across a battery of 3.0 V by means of a wire of negligible resistance. A current of 0.5 A passes through the resistor. Calculate (a) Power dissipated in the resistor.

(b) Total power produced by the battery. (c) Give the reason of difference between these two quantities.

Step 1: (a) Power in resistor = I^2 x R = (0.5)^2 x 5.6 = 0.25 x 5.6 = 1.4 W.

Step 2: (b) Total power = V x I = 3.0 x 0.5 = 1.5 W.

Step 3: (c) The difference of 0.1 W is lost as heat in the internal resistance of the battery.

Final answer: (a) 1.4 W (b) 1.5 W (c) power lost in internal resistance.

Magnetic poles do not affect each other

options: From north pole to south pole
From south pole to north pole
There are no field lines inside a magnet
mcqs.why: Outside the magnet the field lines run from north to south; inside the magnet they continue from the south pole to the north pole, forming closed loops.

mcqs.why: A magnetic compass needle is a small magnet that turns to align with any magnetic field present. A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force.

mcqs.q: If the current in a wire placed perpendicular to a magnetic field increases, the force on the wire
mcqs.why: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field grows with the current: a larger current means more charge carriers being pushed by the field.

mcqs.q: A D.C. motor converts
mcqs.why: In a D.C. motor, current in a coil placed in a magnetic field produces a torque that rotates the coil, turning electrical energy into mechanical rotation.

mcqs.q: Which part of a D.C. motor reverses the direction of current through the coil every half-cycle?
mcqs.why: The split-ring commutator swaps the coil's connections every half turn, reversing the current so the torque keeps acting in the same direction. Slip rings are used in A.C. generators instead.

mcqs.q: The direction of the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is in accordance with the conservation of
mcqs.why: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change producing it, so work must be done against this opposition; that work becomes the electrical energy, and energy is conserved.

mcqs.q: A step-up transformer
options: Has more turns in the primary coil
Has fewer turns in the secondary coil
mcqs.why: A step-up transformer has more turns on its secondary than on its primary, so Vs/Vp = Ns/Np is greater than 1 and the output voltage is higher than the input voltage.

mcqs.q: The turn ratio of a transformer is 10. This means
mcqs.why: Turn ratio 10 means the secondary has ten times as many turns as the primary, Ns = 10 x Np, so the secondary voltage is also ten times the primary voltage.

mcqs.q: In a step-up transformer, compared with the primary coil, the secondary coil has
mcqs.why: Since Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, raising the voltage requires Ns greater than Np: the secondary of a step-up transformer is wound with more turns than the primary.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
15.1. Demonstrate by an experiment that a magnetic field is produced around a straight current-carrying conductor.

Pass a straight wire vertically through a horizontal card and sprinkle iron filings on the card. With no current, the filings lie randomly. When current flows through the wire, the filings arrange themselves in concentric circles around the wire, and a compass needle placed near the wire deflects. This shows a magnetic field exists around the current-carrying conductor.

15.2. State and explain the rule by which the direction of the lines of force of the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor can be determined.

The right-hand grip rule gives the direction: grip the conductor with the right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the current; the curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines around the conductor. Reversing the current reverses the field direction.

15.3. You are given an unmarked magnetized steel bar and a bar magnet, its north and south ends are marked N and S respectively. State how you would determine the polarity at each end of the unmarked bar.

Bring one end of the unmarked bar near the N end of the marked magnet. If it is repelled, that end is also north, because like poles repel; if it is attracted, that end is south. Test the other end the same way to confirm: the end attracted to N is south and the end repelled by N is north.

15.4. When a straight current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. State the rule by which the direction of this force can be found out.

Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction: hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand mutually at right angles. The first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field, the second finger in the direction of the current, and the thumb then points in the direction of the force on the conductor.

15.5. State that a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque.

When a rectangular coil carrying current is placed in a magnetic field, the two opposite sides of the coil experience equal and opposite forces in different directions, forming a couple. This couple produces a torque that rotates the coil. The torque is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field and zero when it is perpendicular to it.

15.6. What is an electric motor? Explain the working principle of D.C motor.

An electric motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. In a D.C. motor, a coil (armature) is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows through the coil, the magnetic field exerts a torque on it and it rotates. The commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the torque always acts in the same direction and the coil keeps rotating.

15.7. Describe a simple experiment to demonstrate that a changing magnetic field can induce e.m.f. in a circuit.

Connect a coil to a sensitive galvanometer and push a bar magnet into the coil. The galvanometer deflects while the magnet moves, showing an induced e.m.f., and returns to zero when the magnet stops. Pulling the magnet out deflects the needle the other way, and moving it faster gives a larger deflection. This proves that a changing magnetic field induces e.m.f.

15.8. What are the factors which affect the magnitude of the e.m.f. induced in a circuit by a changing magnetic field?

The induced e.m.f. depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux: faster movement of the magnet or coil gives larger e.m.f. It also depends on the strength of the magnet, the number of turns in the coil, and the area of the coil. Increasing any of these increases the induced e.m.f., as stated by Faraday's law.

15.9. Describe the direction of an induced e.m.f. in a circuit. How does this phenomenon relate to conservation of energy?

Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change that produced it. For example, pushing a magnet into a coil induces a current whose magnetic field repels the magnet, so work must be done against this repulsion. That work becomes the electrical energy of the induced current, so energy is conserved and cannot be created from nothing.

15.10. Draw a labelled diagram to illustrate the structure and working of A.C generator.

Draw a rectangular coil between the poles of a magnet, with its ends connected to two slip rings and brushes leading to an external circuit. As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux through it changes, inducing an alternating e.m.f. that reverses direction every half turn. Label the coil, magnet poles, slip rings, brushes and load.

15.11. What do you understand by the term mutual induction?

Mutual induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil. The changing current produces a changing magnetic field, and this changing flux links with the second coil, inducing an e.m.f. in it. It is the principle on which transformers work.

15.12. What is a transformer? Explain the working of a transformer in connection with mutual induction.

A transformer is a device that changes alternating voltage from one value to another without changing frequency. It has a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on a soft iron core. Alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links with the secondary coil and induces an alternating voltage there by mutual induction. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

15.13. The voltage chosen for the transmission of electrical power over large distances is many times greater than the voltage of the domestic supply. State two reasons why electrical power is transmitted at high voltage.

Power is transmitted at high voltage for two reasons. First, for a given power, higher voltage means lower current (P = VI), and lower current means much less heat loss in the wires (loss = I^2 R). Second, lower current allows thinner, cheaper wires to be used and reduces the voltage drop along the line.

15.14. Why is the voltage used for the domestic supply much lower than the voltage at which the power is transmitted?

Domestic supply is kept low, at 220 V, because high voltage is extremely dangerous in homes and would damage ordinary appliances, which are designed for low voltage. High transmission voltage is therefore stepped down by transformers at substations to a safe value before it enters houses.

mcqs.why: With current flowing, the filings form concentric circles around the wire and a nearby compass needle deflects, demonstrating that a magnetic field exists around a current-carrying conductor.

mcqs.q: By the right-hand grip rule, if the thumb points in the direction of the current, the curled fingers point in the direction of
options: The magnetic field lines around the conductor
mcqs.why: Grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb along the current: the curled fingers give the direction of the circular magnetic field. Reversing the current reverses the field.

mcqs.q: To find the polarity of an unmarked magnetized bar using a marked magnet, the reliable test is repulsion: an end that is repelled by the marked N pole is
mcqs.why: Only like poles repel. If the marked north pole repels the end of the unmarked bar, that end must also be north; an end attracted to N would be south.

mcqs.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the first finger, second finger and thumb point respectively in the directions of
options: Magnetic field, current, and force on the conductor
mcqs.why: With the three digits held mutually at right angles: first finger = Field, second finger = Current, thumb = Motion (the force on the conductor).

mcqs.q: A current-carrying rectangular coil in a magnetic field experiences the greatest torque when
options: The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
The current in the coil is zero
The plane of the coil is parallel to the field
The coil has only one turn
mcqs.why: The opposite sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions and experience equal and opposite forces forming a couple. This torque is greatest when the coil's plane is parallel to the field and zero when perpendicular.

mcqs.q: In a D.C. motor the coil keeps rotating in the same direction because
options: The brushes increase the current steadily
The magnet poles swap every half turn
The coil is pushed by the slip rings
The commutator reverses the current every half turn, keeping the torque in the same direction
mcqs.why: Without reversal, the torque would reverse each half turn and the coil would only oscillate. The commutator reverses the current just as the coil passes the vertical position.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the e.m.f. induced by a changing magnetic field increases with
options: The rate of change of magnetic flux, the strength of the magnet, and the number of turns of the coil
Only the resistance of the circuit
The thickness of the wire alone
The time the magnet stays still in the coil
mcqs.why: By Faraday's law the induced e.m.f. depends on how fast the flux changes, and it also grows with a stronger magnet, more turns and a larger coil area. A stationary magnet induces nothing.

mcqs.q: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is such that it
options: Helps the change that produced it
Opposes the change that produced it
Is the same as the inducing current
mcqs.why: Pushing a magnet into a coil induces a current whose field repels the magnet, so work is done against the repulsion and becomes electrical energy, conserving energy.

mcqs.q: In an A.C. generator, the ends of the rotating coil are connected to the external circuit through
mcqs.why: Each end of the coil is joined to a slip ring that rotates with it, and brushes press on the rings to take the alternating e.m.f. to the external circuit without reversing the connections.

mcqs.q: Electrical power is transmitted over large distances at high voltage because, for a given power, higher voltage means lower current, and lower current means
options: More heat loss in the wires
Thicker and costlier wires are needed
The frequency of the supply increases
Much less heat loss in the wires, since loss = I^2 x R
mcqs.why: From P = V x I, raising V lowers I for the same power, and the heating loss I^2 x R falls sharply. Lower current also allows thinner, cheaper wires and reduces the voltage drop along the line.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
15.1. Suppose someone handed you three similar iron bars and told you one was not a magnet, but the other two were. How would you find the iron bar that was not a magnet?

Use the repulsion test: only magnets repel each other. Take any two bars and bring their ends together in all combinations. The bar that is never repelled by either of the other two, but only attracted, is the unmagnetized iron bar, because attraction can occur between a magnet and iron, while repulsion occurs only between two magnets.

15.2. Suppose you have a coil of wire and a bar magnet. Describe how you could use them to generate an electric current.

Connect the coil to a galvanometer and move the bar magnet in and out of the coil. The changing magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. in the coil and a current flows, shown by the galvanometer deflection. Moving the magnet faster, or using a coil with more turns, gives a larger current.

15.3. Which device is used for converting electrical energy into mechanical energy?

An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Examples are the motors in fans, washing machines, electric trains and water pumps, where current in a coil in a magnetic field produces rotation.

15.4. Suppose we hang a loop of wire so that it can swing easily. If we now put a magnet into the coil, the coil will start swinging. Which way will it swing relative to the magnet, and why?

The coil swings away from the approaching magnet. By Lenz's law, the current induced in the coil produces a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet, so the coil is repelled. The coil therefore moves away from the magnet that is being pushed towards it.

15.5. A conductor wire generates a voltage while moving through a magnetic field. In what direction should the wire be moved, relative to the field to generate the maximum voltage?

The wire should be moved at right angles to the magnetic field, cutting the field lines as fast as possible. The induced e.m.f. is greatest when the motion is perpendicular to the field, and zero when the wire moves parallel to the field lines without cutting them.

15.6. What is the difference between a generator and a motor?

A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy: rotating a coil in a magnetic field induces an e.m.f. A motor does the reverse: it converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, as current in a coil in a magnetic field produces rotation. Both use the same electromagnetic principles in opposite directions.

15.7. What reverses the direction of electric current in the armature coil of D.C motor?

The commutator (split ring) reverses the current in the armature coil every half turn. As the coil rotates, each half of the split ring changes contact from one brush to the other, so the current through the coil reverses direction just as the coil passes the vertical position, keeping the torque in the same direction.

15.8. A wire lying perpendicular to an external magnetic field carries current in the direction shown in the diagram. In what direction will the wire move due to the resulting magnetic force?

Apply Fleming's left-hand rule: with the field pointing from N to S (left to right in the diagram) and the current flowing as shown, the thumb points in the direction of the force. The wire therefore moves at right angles to both the field and the current, in the direction given by the left-hand rule for the diagram's field and current directions.

15.9. Can a transformer operate on direct current?

No, a transformer cannot work on direct current. It needs a changing magnetic flux to induce a voltage in the secondary coil, and direct current produces a steady, unchanging flux once switched on. Only alternating current, which continually changes, produces the changing flux needed for mutual induction.

mcqs.q: Given three similar iron bars, two magnetized and one not, the bar that is NOT a magnet can be identified as the one that
options: Attracts both other bars most strongly
Is never repelled by either of the other two bars, but only attracted
mcqs.why: Repulsion occurs only between two magnets, while a magnet also attracts plain iron. Testing all combinations, the bar that is only ever attracted and never repelled is the unmagnetized iron bar.

mcqs.q: To generate an electric current with a coil and a bar magnet, you should
options: Connect the coil to a galvanometer and move the magnet in and out of the coil
Hold the magnet perfectly still inside the coil
Connect the coil to a battery
Heat the coil with the magnet nearby
mcqs.why: The changing magnetic flux through the coil induces an e.m.f. and a current, shown by the galvanometer. Moving the magnet faster, or using more turns, gives a larger current.

mcqs.q: Which device converts electrical energy into mechanical energy in fans, washing machines and water pumps?
mcqs.why: An electric motor uses the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field to produce rotation, converting electrical energy into mechanical energy.

mcqs.q: A loop of wire hangs so it can swing freely. When a magnet is pushed into the coil, the coil swings
options: Towards the magnet, because the induced current attracts it
Away from the magnet, because the induced current's field repels it
Not at all, since the loop is open
mcqs.why: By Lenz's law the induced current makes the coil's near end a pole like the approaching pole of the magnet, so the coil is repelled and swings away, opposing the change that produced the current.

mcqs.q: A wire moving through a magnetic field generates the maximum voltage when it is moved
options: Only when the field is switched off
At right angles to the magnetic field, cutting the field lines as fast as possible
mcqs.why: The induced e.m.f. depends on how fast the wire cuts the field lines: it is greatest for motion perpendicular to the field and zero when the wire moves parallel to the lines without cutting them.

mcqs.q: A generator and a motor differ in that
options: A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy, while a motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy
A generator uses D.C. and a motor uses A.C. only
A motor has no magnet in it
A generator produces motion from current
mcqs.why: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field induces an e.m.f. (generator), while passing current through a coil in a magnetic field produces rotation (motor). They use the same principles in opposite directions.

mcqs.q: In a D.C. motor, the direction of current in the armature coil is reversed every half turn by
mcqs.why: As the coil rotates, each half of the split ring changes contact from one brush to the other just as the coil passes the vertical position, reversing the current and keeping the torque in one direction.

mcqs.q: A transformer cannot operate on direct current because direct current produces
options: Too much voltage in the secondary
A changing flux in the wrong direction
A steady, unchanging magnetic flux, so no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil
mcqs.why: Mutual induction needs a continually changing flux. Once switched on, D.C. gives a constant flux in the core, so nothing is induced in the secondary; only A.C. works.

mcqs.q: The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field acts in a direction that is
options: At right angles to both the field and the current
mcqs.why: Fleming's left-hand rule holds the thumb, first finger and second finger mutually at right angles: field and current along two fingers, and the thumb gives the force, perpendicular to both.

mcqs.q: Moving a magnet faster in and out of a coil produces
mcqs.why: Faster movement changes the magnetic flux more rapidly, and by Faraday's law a faster rate of change of flux induces a larger e.m.f. and current, seen as a bigger galvanometer deflection.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
15.1. A transformer is needed to convert a mains 240 V supply into a 12 V supply. If there are 2000 turns on the primary coil, then find the number of turns on the secondary coil.

Step 1: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Ns = Np x Vs/Vp.

Step 2: Ns = 2000 x 12/240 = 2000 x 0.05 = 100.

Final answer: Secondary turns = 100.

15.2. A step-up transformer has a turn ratio of 1:100.

An alternating supply of 20 V is connected across the primary coil. What is the secondary voltage?

Step 1: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = 100/1 = 100.

Step 2: Vs = 100 x Vp = 100 x 20 = 2000 V.

Final answer: Secondary voltage = 2000 V.

15.3. A step-down transformer has a turns ratio of 100:1. An a.c. voltage of amplitude 170 V is applied to the primary. If the current in the primary is 1.0 mA, what is the current in the secondary?

Step 1: For an ideal transformer, Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, and Vs = Vp x (1/100) = 1.7 V.

Step 2: Is = (Vp x Ip) / Vs = (170 x 0.001) / 1.7 = 0.17 / 1.7 = 0.1 A.

Final answer: Secondary current = 0.1 A.

15.4. A transformer, designed to convert the voltage from 240 V a.c. mains to 12 V, has 4000 turns on the primary coil. How many turns should be on the secondary coil? If the transformer were 100% efficient, what current would flow through the primary coil when the current in the secondary coil was 0.4 A?

Step 1: Ns = Np x Vs/Vp = 4000 x 12/240 = 200 turns.

Step 2: For 100% efficiency, Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Ip = (Vs x Is)/Vp = (12 x 0.4)/240 = 4.8/240 = 0.02 A.

Final answer: Secondary turns = 200; primary current = 0.02 A.

15.5. A power station generates 500 MW of electrical power which is fed to a transmission line. What current would flow in the transmission line, if the input voltage is 250 kV?

Step 1: P = V x I, so I = P/V.

Step 2: P = 500 MW = 500 x 10^6 W; V = 250 kV = 250 x 10^3 V.

Step 3: I = (500 x 10^6) / (250 x 10^3) = 2000 A = 2 x 10^3 A.

Final answer: Current = 2 x 10^3 A.

mcqs.why: For an ideal transformer Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Is = (Vp x Ip) / Vs = (170 x 0.001) / 1.7 = 0.17 / 1.7 = 0.1 A.

That transformer is 100% efficient and the secondary current is 0.4 A. The primary current is
mcqs.why: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Ip = (Vs x Is) / Vp = (12 x 0.4) / 240 = 4.8 / 240 = 0.02 A.

mcqs.q: A power station generates 500 MW fed to a transmission line at 250 kV. The current in the line is
If the same 500 MW were transmitted at 500 kV instead of 250 kV, the current in the line would be
mcqs.why: I = P / V = (500 x 10^6) / (500 x 10^3) = 1000 A. Doubling the transmission voltage halves the current for the same power, which is why high voltage reduces losses.

mcqs.q: For the 240 V to 12 V transformer, the ratio Vs / Vp is
mcqs.why: Vs / Vp = 12 / 240 = 0.05 = 1 / 20. The same ratio gives the turns ratio Ns / Np, so the secondary needs only one-twentieth as many turns as the primary.

mcqs.q: In an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, the input power and output power are related as
options: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
Vp x Is = Vs x Ip
mcqs.why: An ideal transformer loses no energy, so the power taken from the primary, Vp x Ip, equals the power delivered by the secondary, Vs x Is. This is the relation used to find unknown currents in transformer problems.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
16.1. Describe, using one simple diagram in each case, what happens when a narrow beam of electrons is passed through (a) a uniform electric field (b) a uniform magnetic field. What do these results indicate about the charge on electron?

In a uniform electric field, the electron beam bends towards the positive plate, showing that electrons carry negative charge. In a uniform magnetic field, the beam bends in a circular path at right angles to both its motion and the field. Both deflections together confirm that cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles.

16.2. Explain the working of different parts of oscilloscope.

An oscilloscope (CRO) has an electron gun that produces a narrow beam of electrons by thermionic emission, focusing anodes that sharpen the beam, deflecting plates that move the beam vertically and horizontally according to the input voltage, and a fluorescent screen that glows where the beam strikes. The beam traces the waveform of the input signal on the screen.

16.3. Name some uses of oscilloscope.

An oscilloscope is used to display and measure alternating voltages and waveforms, to find the frequency and amplitude of a signal, to study sound waves and heartbeats, to test radio and television circuits, and to observe signals that change too fast for an ordinary meter to follow.

16.4. Considering an oscilloscope explain: (i) How the filament is heated? (ii) Why the filament is heated? (iii) Why the anode potential is kept positive with respect to the cathode potential? (iv) Why a large potential is applied between anode and cathode? (v) Why the tube is evacuated?

(i) The filament is heated by passing an electric current through it. (ii) Heating causes thermionic emission, releasing electrons from the cathode. (iii) The anode is kept positive so that it attracts the negatively charged electrons towards the screen. (iv) A large potential gives the electrons high speed, making a bright, sharp spot on the screen. (v) The tube is evacuated so the electrons do not collide with air molecules on their way to the screen.

16.5. What is electron gun? Describe the process of thermionic emission.

An electron gun is the part of a cathode ray tube that produces and focuses a beam of electrons. In thermionic emission, a metal cathode is heated until its free electrons gain enough energy to escape from the metal surface. These emitted electrons are then accelerated by a positive anode to form a beam.

16.6. What do you understand by digital and analogue quantities?

An analogue quantity changes continuously over a range, for example temperature, sound loudness or the position of a clock hand. A digital quantity changes in separate steps and takes only definite values, for example the numbers on a digital clock or the on/off states 0 and 1 in a computer.

16.7. Differentiate between analogue electronics and digital electronics. Write down names of five analogue and five digital devices that are commonly used in everyday life.

Analogue electronics deals with signals that vary continuously, while digital electronics deals with signals that have only two states, 0 and 1. Five analogue devices are: a mercury thermometer, a moving-coil voltmeter, a vinyl record player, an analogue wristwatch and a microphone. Five digital devices are: a digital watch, a calculator, a computer, a mobile phone and a digital camera.

16.8. State and explain for each case whether the information given by the following devices is in analogue or a digital form. a. a moving-coil voltmeter measuring the e.m.f of a cell. b. a microphone generating an electric current. c. a central heating thermostat controlling the water pump. d. automatic traffic lights controlling the flow of traffic.

(a) Analogue: the needle moves continuously with the voltage. (b) Analogue: the current varies continuously with the sound pressure. (c) Digital: the thermostat switches the pump either on or off at a set temperature. (d) Digital: the lights are in one of a few fixed states (red, yellow, green) changed in steps.

16.9. Write down some benefits of using digital electronics over analogue electronics.

Digital electronics is more accurate because values are stored as exact numbers, less affected by noise because only two states must be distinguished, easier to store and copy without loss of quality, cheaper to build with integrated circuits, and able to process, transmit and display information very quickly.

16.10. What are the three universal Logic Gates? Give their symbols and truth tables.

The three universal logic gates are NAND, NOR and NOT-combined gates: NAND and NOR are called universal because any other logic function can be built from NAND gates alone or from NOR gates alone. NAND: output is 0 only when both inputs are 1, otherwise 1. NOR: output is 1 only when both inputs are 0, otherwise 0. NOT: output is the opposite of the input, 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.

mcqs.q: A narrow beam of electrons passing through a uniform electric field bends towards the positive plate. This indicates that electrons
mcqs.why: A negative charge is attracted to a positive plate. The deflection of the beam towards the positive plate, and its bending in a magnetic field, show cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles.

mcqs.q: In an oscilloscope, the electron gun produces a narrow beam of electrons by
options: Thermionic emission from a heated cathode
mcqs.why: The electron gun heats the cathode until electrons escape by thermionic emission; focusing anodes sharpen the beam, deflecting plates steer it, and the fluorescent screen glows where it strikes.

mcqs.q: The filament of an oscilloscope is heated by passing an electric current through it, and the heating is needed because it
options: Melts the cathode into a beam shape
Causes thermionic emission, releasing electrons from the cathode
mcqs.why: Heating the cathode gives its free electrons enough energy to escape the metal surface. Without this emission there would be no electron beam to trace the signal.

mcqs.q: In the oscilloscope tube, a large potential is applied between anode and cathode in order to
options: Give the electrons high speed, making a bright, sharp spot on the screen
Stop the electrons at the anode
mcqs.why: The anode is kept positive so it attracts the negatively charged electrons, and a large potential accelerates them strongly so the spot on the fluorescent screen is bright and sharp.

mcqs.q: The tube of an oscilloscope is evacuated (air removed) so that
options: The screen can glow more cheaply
The filament does not burn out in a day
The electrons do not collide with air molecules on their way to the screen
mcqs.why: In a vacuum the beam travels in a clean path from the electron gun to the screen; air molecules would scatter the electrons and blur or stop the beam.

mcqs.q: An analogue quantity differs from a digital quantity in that an analogue quantity
options: Changes continuously over a range, while a digital quantity changes in separate steps with definite values
mcqs.why: Temperature, sound loudness and the position of a clock hand vary continuously (analogue), while the numbers on a digital clock or the on/off states 0 and 1 change in steps (digital).

mcqs.q: Which of the following devices gives its information in digital form?
options: A moving-coil voltmeter measuring a cell
A central heating thermostat switching the pump on or off
mcqs.why: The thermostat is either on or off at the set temperature, a two-state (digital) output. The moving-coil voltmeter's needle and the microphone's current vary continuously, so they are analogue.

mcqs.q: One benefit of digital electronics over analogue electronics is that digital signals are
options: Less affected by noise, because only two states must be distinguished
Faster than the speed of light
mcqs.why: With only 0 and 1 to tell apart, small disturbances do not change the value. Digital information is also accurate, easy to store and copy without loss, and quick to process and transmit.

mcqs.q: NAND and NOR gates are called universal gates because
options: They are used in every country
They have the largest number of inputs
They were the first gates invented
Any other logic function can be built from NAND gates alone or from NOR gates alone
mcqs.why: The three universal gates discussed in the book are built around NAND, NOR and NOT: since every logic operation can be assembled from NANDs alone or NORs alone, they are called universal.

mcqs.q: The NOT gate is the one whose output is
options: The opposite of the input: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1
mcqs.why: NOT is the inverter: it has a single input and gives the complement as output, turning 1 into 0 and 0 into 1.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
16.1. Name two factors which can enhance thermionic emission.

Thermionic emission is enhanced by increasing the temperature of the cathode, which gives more electrons enough energy to escape, and by using a cathode material with a low work function, such as coated metals, from which electrons escape more easily.

16.2. Give three reasons to support the evidence that cathode rays are negatively charged electrons.

Cathode rays bend towards a positively charged plate in an electric field, showing they are negative. They bend in a magnetic field in the direction expected for negative charges. They also carry the same charge-to-mass ratio wherever they are produced, showing they are identical particles, the electrons.

16.3. When electrons pass through two parallel plates having opposite charges, they are deflected towards the positively charged plate.

What important characteristic of the electron can be inferred from this? The deflection towards the positive plate shows that the electron carries a negative electric charge, because a negative charge is attracted to a positive plate and repelled by a negative plate. This is direct evidence of the negative charge of the electron.

16.4. When a moving electron enters the magnetic field, it is deflected from its straight path. Name two factors which can enhance electron deflection.

Electron deflection in a magnetic field is increased by a stronger magnetic field and by a higher speed of the electron (up to the point where it leaves the field). A longer region of field also gives the electron more time to bend, increasing the total deflection.

16.5. How can you compare the logic operation X = A.B with usual operation of multiplication?

The logic operation X = A.B behaves exactly like ordinary multiplication of 0 and 1: 0 x 0 = 0, 0 x 1 = 0, 1 x 0 = 0, and 1 x 1 = 1. The output is 1 only when both inputs are 1, just as a product is non-zero only when both factors are non-zero.

16.6. NAND gate is the reciprocal of AND gate. Discuss.

A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by a NOT gate, so its output is the opposite (complement) of the AND output. Where AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, NAND gives 0 in that case and 1 in all other cases. NAND is therefore the inverted, or reciprocal, form of AND.

16.7. Show that the circuit given below acts as OR gate.

The circuit in the book combines gates so that its output is 1 whenever either input A or input B is 1, and 0 only when both are 0. Writing the truth table for the combination gives: 0,0 gives 0; 0,1 gives 1; 1,0 gives 1; 1,1 gives 1. This is exactly the truth table of an OR gate, so the circuit acts as an OR gate.

16.8. Show that the circuit given below acts as AND gate.

The circuit in the book combines gates so that its output is 1 only when both inputs A and B are 1, and 0 in all other cases. Its truth table is: 0,0 gives 0; 0,1 gives 0; 1,0 gives 0; 1,1 gives 1. This is exactly the truth table of an AND gate, so the circuit acts as an AND gate.

mcqs.q: Thermionic emission is enhanced by
options: Increasing the temperature of the cathode and using a cathode material with a low work function
Cooling the cathode and using a thick metal
Reducing the anode potential to zero
Covering the cathode with an insulator
mcqs.why: Higher temperature gives more electrons enough energy to escape, and a low work-function material, such as a coated metal, lets electrons escape more easily.

mcqs.q: Which observation supports the evidence that cathode rays are negatively charged?
options: They travel in straight lines in a vacuum
They bend towards a positively charged plate in an electric field
They make a fluorescent screen glow
They are produced by a hot cathode
mcqs.why: Attraction to the positive plate shows the rays carry negative charge. They also bend in a magnetic field as negative charges should, and have the same charge-to-mass ratio wherever produced.

mcqs.q: Electrons passing between two oppositely charged parallel plates are deflected towards the positively charged plate. The important characteristic of the electron inferred from this is that
options: The electron has a very large mass
The electron is a wave only
The electron carries a negative electric charge
The electron moves at the speed of light
mcqs.why: A negative charge is attracted to a positive plate and repelled by a negative plate, so this deflection is direct evidence of the electron's negative charge.

mcqs.q: The deflection of a moving electron in a magnetic field is increased by
options: A weaker magnetic field and slower electrons
Making the electron stop inside the field
A stronger magnetic field and a higher speed of the electron
mcqs.why: A stronger field pushes the electron harder sideways, and a faster electron (within the field) is deflected more; a longer region of field also gives more time to bend and increases the total deflection.

mcqs.q: The logic operation X = A.B can be compared with ordinary multiplication because
options: 0 x 0 = 0, 0 x 1 = 0, 1 x 0 = 0 and 1 x 1 = 1, exactly the AND truth table
The output is 1 whenever any input is 1
mcqs.why: Multiplying the possible values of A and B gives 1 only when both factors are 1, which is precisely the behaviour of the AND gate X = A.B.

mcqs.q: A NAND gate is the reciprocal (inverted form) of an AND gate because it is
options: An AND gate followed by a NOT gate, giving the opposite output in every case
An AND gate with its inputs swapped
An AND gate that works on three inputs
mcqs.why: Where AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, NAND gives 0 in that case and 1 in all others: its output is the complement of the AND output at every row of the truth table.

mcqs.q: A combination of gates whose truth table is 0,0 gives 0; 0,1 gives 1; 1,0 gives 1; 1,1 gives 1 acts as
mcqs.why: Output 1 whenever either input is 1, and 0 only when both are 0, is exactly the truth table of the OR gate, so the circuit acts as an OR gate.

mcqs.q: A combination of gates whose truth table is 0,0 gives 0; 0,1 gives 0; 1,0 gives 0; 1,1 gives 1 acts as
mcqs.why: Output 1 only when both inputs A and B are 1, and 0 in all other cases, is exactly the truth table of the AND gate.

mcqs.q: Cathode rays produced in different tubes have the same charge-to-mass ratio everywhere. This shows that the particles are
mcqs.why: Whatever the tube or gas used, cathode rays show the same charge-to-mass ratio, proving they are one kind of particle, the electron, a constituent of all atoms.

mcqs.q: An electron spends more time inside a magnetic field region when the region is longer. The result is that its total deflection
mcqs.why: The sideways magnetic force acts for a longer time on an electron crossing a longer field region, so the beam bends further and the total deflection is greater.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
17.1. What is difference between data and information?

Data are raw, unorganized facts and figures, such as a list of marks, which by themselves have no clear meaning. Information is data that has been processed, organized and presented in a useful form, such as a result card showing each student's total and position, from which decisions can be made.

17.2. What do you understand by Information and Communication Technology (ICT)?

Information and Communication Technology is the use of computers, telecommunication and other electronic systems to store, process, retrieve and communicate information. It includes hardware, software, networks, the internet, mobile phones and broadcasting, all used to handle information quickly and over long distances.

17.3. What are the components of information technology?

Clearly indicate the function of each component. The main components are: input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner) that feed data into the computer; the CPU that processes data; memory that stores data and programs; output devices (monitor, printer) that present information; storage devices (hard disk, flash drive) that keep data for later use; and communication devices (modem, network card) that send and receive data.

17.4. Differentiate between the primary memory and the secondary memory.

Primary memory (RAM and ROM) works directly with the CPU, is fast, and is limited in size; RAM is temporary and loses its contents when power is off, while ROM keeps its contents. Secondary memory (hard disk, flash drive, DVD) is slower but much larger and permanent, keeping data even when the power is off.

17.5. Name different information storage devices and describe their uses.

Storage devices include the hard disk, which stores large amounts of data inside a computer; the flash drive (USB), which carries data portably between computers; the compact disc and DVD, which store music, video and software; the memory card, used in cameras and phones; and magnetic tape, used for backing up large amounts of data.

17.6. Explain briefly the transmission of radiowaves through space.

Radiowaves are electromagnetic waves produced by alternating currents in an antenna. They travel through space at the speed of light without needing a medium, are reflected by the ionosphere for long-distance short-wave broadcasts, or travel in straight lines for television and satellite links. A receiving antenna converts the waves back into electrical signals.

17.7. How are light signals sent through optical fibre?

Light signals are sent through an optical fibre by total internal reflection. A laser or LED flashes coded pulses of light into one end of the thin glass fibre, and the light reflects repeatedly from the inner walls without escaping, following the fibre's path until it reaches a detector at the far end, which converts it back into an electrical signal.

17.8. What is computer? What is the role of computer in everyday life?

A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data, processes it according to instructions, and gives out information. In everyday life it is used for education, business, banking, communication, entertainment, medicine, transport and government, making work faster, more accurate and easier to store and share.

17.9. What is the difference between hardware and software? Name different softwares.

Hardware is the physical part of a computer that can be touched, such as the keyboard, monitor, CPU and printer. Software is the set of programs and instructions that tells the hardware what to do and cannot be touched. Different softwares are: operating systems (Windows, Android), word processors, spreadsheets, web browsers, and media players.

17.10. What do you understand by the term word processing and data managing?

Word processing is the use of a computer program to create, edit, format, store and print documents, such as letters and reports. Data managing is the organizing, storing, updating and retrieving of large collections of data, usually in a database, so that information can be found, sorted and used quickly and accurately.

17.11. What is Internet?

Internet is a useful source of knowledge and information. Discuss. The internet is a worldwide network of millions of interconnected computers that share information using common rules. It is a vast source of knowledge because it gives instant access to books, research, news, courses, maps and expert advice from around the world, and allows people to learn, communicate and work together across distances.

17.12. Discuss the role of information technology in school education.

Information technology in schools provides digital textbooks, videos and simulations that make learning clearer, allows students to research topics online, helps teachers prepare lessons and keep records, enables online classes and tests, and develops computer skills that students need for further study and work.

mcqs.q: Data differ from information in that data are
options: Raw, unorganized facts, while information is data processed into a useful form
Always numbers, while information is always text
mcqs.why: A list of marks is data; a result card showing totals and positions, from which decisions can be made, is information. Information is data that has been processed, organized and presented usefully.

mcqs.q: In the components of information technology, the function of input devices such as the keyboard, mouse and scanner is to
mcqs.why: Input devices feed data in; the CPU processes it; memory stores data and programs; output devices such as the monitor and printer present information; and communication devices send and receive data.

mcqs.q: Primary memory differs from secondary memory in that primary memory
options: Is slower but much larger and permanent
Works directly with the CPU, is fast and limited, and RAM loses its contents when the power is off
Keeps data even without power in all cases
mcqs.why: Primary memory (RAM and ROM) is fast and works directly with the CPU; RAM is temporary while ROM keeps its contents. Secondary memory such as a hard disk is slower but much larger and permanent.

mcqs.q: Secondary memory, such as a hard disk or flash drive, is used because it
options: Loses data when the power is off
Keeps data permanently, even when the power is off
mcqs.why: Secondary storage holds data and programs for later use with the power off, unlike RAM. A flash drive also carries data portably between computers.

mcqs.q: Radiowaves used for long-distance short-wave broadcasts reach far stations because they are
mcqs.why: Radiowaves are electromagnetic waves produced by alternating currents in an antenna. They travel through space at the speed of light, and the ionosphere reflects them back for long-distance short-wave communication.

mcqs.q: Light signals are sent through an optical fibre by
options: Refraction out of the fibre at every bend
Total internal reflection, the light bouncing repeatedly along the inside of the fibre
Travelling through the glass as electric current
Being absorbed and re-emitted by the glass
mcqs.why: Coded pulses of light from a laser or LED enter one end of the thin fibre and reflect repeatedly from the inner walls without escaping, until a detector at the far end converts them back into electrical signals.

mcqs.q: Hardware differs from software in that hardware is
options: The programs that run the computer
The physical part of the computer that can be touched, while software is the set of programs and instructions
Unable to work without being touched by programs only
mcqs.why: The keyboard, monitor, CPU and printer are hardware. Software, such as operating systems (Windows, Android), word processors, spreadsheets and browsers, tells the hardware what to do and cannot be touched.

mcqs.q: Word processing means using a computer program to
options: Manage a database of thousands of records
Create, edit, format, store and print documents such as letters and reports
mcqs.why: Word processing is the production of documents with a program. Data managing, by contrast, is organizing, storing, updating and retrieving large collections of data, usually in a database.

mcqs.q: The Internet is best described as
options: A worldwide network of millions of interconnected computers sharing information by common rules
A single large computer in one country
mcqs.why: The internet links computers across the world, giving instant access to books, research, news, courses, maps and expert advice, and letting people learn, communicate and work together across distances.

mcqs.q: One role of information technology in school education is that it
options: Replaces the need for students entirely
Provides digital textbooks, videos and simulations that make learning clearer
mcqs.why: IT also lets students research topics online, helps teachers prepare lessons and keep records, enables online classes and tests, and develops the computer skills students need for further study and work.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
17.1. Why is optical fibre a more useful tool for the communication process?

Optical fibre is more useful because light signals in a fibre suffer very little loss and interference, can carry far more information at higher speed than copper wires, are light and thin, and are secure because the signal is hard to tap. One fibre can therefore carry thousands of telephone calls or television channels at once.

17.2. Which is more reliable, floppy disk or a hard disk?

A hard disk is more reliable than a floppy disk. It is sealed inside a protective case, stores much more data, reads and writes faster, and is less easily damaged by dust, bending or magnetic fields. Floppy disks are fragile, hold very little data, and lose data easily.

17.3. What is the difference between RAM and ROM memories?

RAM (Random Access Memory) is temporary, fast memory that the CPU uses while working; its contents are lost when the computer is switched off, and data can be both read and written. ROM (Read Only Memory) is permanent memory that keeps its contents without power; it holds the start-up instructions of the computer and normally cannot be changed by the user.

mcqs.q: Optical fibre is a more useful tool for communication than copper wire because light signals in a fibre
options: Suffer very little loss and interference
Can carry only one call at a time
mcqs.why: Signals in a fibre arrive almost undamaged over long distances, so optical fibre communication is clearer and more reliable than electrical signals in copper wires.

mcqs.q: Compared with copper wires, an optical fibre can carry
options: The same information at the same speed
Far more information at higher speed
Only text, not voice or pictures
mcqs.why: The high frequency of light gives the fibre a huge capacity: one fibre can carry thousands of telephone calls or television channels at once, far beyond a copper pair.

mcqs.q: Optical fibre communication is considered secure because
options: The fibre is made of glass
The signals travel at the speed of light
The signal is hard to tap inside the fibre
mcqs.why: Unlike electrical signals in copper wire, which can be picked up from outside, the light signal stays trapped inside the fibre by total internal reflection, so it is very difficult to intercept.

mcqs.q: A hard disk is more reliable than a floppy disk because a hard disk
options: Is sealed inside a protective case and is less easily damaged by dust, bending or magnetic fields
mcqs.why: A hard disk also stores much more data and reads and writes faster. Floppy disks are fragile, hold very little data and lose data easily.

mcqs.q: Floppy disks are unreliable mainly because they are
options: Fragile, hold very little data and lose data easily
mcqs.why: The exposed flexible disk is easily damaged by dust, bending and magnetic fields, and its small capacity makes it unsuitable where reliability matters, unlike the sealed hard disk.

mcqs.q: RAM (Random Access Memory) is the computer's temporary working memory: its contents are
options: Impossible to change by the user
Lost when the computer is switched off, and data in it can be both read and written
mcqs.why: RAM is fast memory that the CPU uses while working. It is volatile: switching off the power clears it, which is why work must be saved to secondary storage.

mcqs.q: ROM (Read Only Memory) differs from RAM in that ROM
options: Loses its contents when the power is off
Is used for temporary working data
Can be freely written by every program
Is permanent memory that keeps its contents without power and holds the computer's start-up instructions
mcqs.why: ROM keeps the start-up (boot) instructions of the computer safe without power and normally cannot be changed by the user, whereas RAM is temporary read-write working memory.

mcqs.q: The start-up instructions of a computer are held in
mcqs.why: ROM is permanent memory whose contents survive without power, so it is used to hold the fixed start-up instructions the computer needs the moment it is switched on.

mcqs.q: Optical fibres are preferred for communication links also because they are
options: Light and thin, so many fibres fit in one cable
Easy to repair by twisting the ends together
mcqs.why: A fibre is a very thin strand of glass or plastic, so a single cable can bundle many fibres, each carrying thousands of calls, while weighing little.

mcqs.q: One fibre can carry thousands of telephone calls or television channels at the same time because
options: Each call uses a separate fibre colour only
The fibre is connected to a satellite
Light signals in the fibre have a very large information-carrying capacity
Copper wires carry the extra calls
mcqs.why: The book's conceptual answer stresses this capacity: light in a fibre carries far more information at higher speed than copper wires, with little loss or interference.
