lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
18.1. What is difference between atomic number and atomic mass number? Give a symbolical representation of a nuclide.

The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus, which decides which element it is. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. A nuclide is written as A over Z before the element symbol, for example carbon-14 is written with mass number 14 and atomic number 6.

18.2. What do you mean by the term radioactivity? Why are some elements radioactive but some are not?

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiations (alpha, beta or gamma) by unstable nuclei as they change into more stable nuclei. Some elements are radioactive because their nuclei have an unstable balance of protons and neutrons, usually too many neutrons, while stable elements have a balanced nucleus that does not need to decay.

18.3. How can we make radioactive elements artificially? Describe with a suitable example.

Radioactive elements can be made artificially by bombarding stable nuclei with neutrons or other particles in a nuclear reactor or accelerator. For example, bombarding stable cobalt-59 with neutrons gives cobalt-60, which is radioactive and is used in medicine and industry.

18.4. What are the three basic radioactive decay processes and how do they differ from each other?

The three processes are alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay. In alpha decay the nucleus emits a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), so mass number falls by 4 and atomic number by 2. In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted, so atomic number rises by 1 with no change in mass number. In gamma decay the nucleus releases energy as a gamma photon, with no change in protons or neutrons.

18.5. Write the alpha decay process for protactinium-234 (atomic number 91). Identify the parent and daughter nuclei in this decay.

Protactinium-234 decays by emitting an alpha particle (mass 4, atomic number 2). The daughter nucleus has mass number 234 - 4 = 230 and atomic number 91 - 2 = 89, which is actinium-230. The parent nucleus is protactinium-234 and the daughter nucleus is actinium-230.

18.6. Explain whether the atomic number can increase during nuclear decay. Support your answer with an example.

Yes, the atomic number can increase during beta decay. In beta decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, so the number of protons rises by one. For example, carbon-14 (6 protons) decays by beta emission into nitrogen-14 (7 protons), so the atomic number increases from 6 to 7.

18.7. What do you understand by half-life of a radioactive element?

The half-life of a radioactive element is the time taken for half of the atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life half the original amount remains, after two half-lives one-quarter remains, and so on. Half-life is a fixed property of each isotope and is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

18.8. Is radioactivity a spontaneous process? Elaborate your answer with a simple experiment.

Yes, radioactivity is a spontaneous process: it happens by itself without any outside cause and cannot be started, stopped or speeded up by ordinary means. In an experiment, a radioactive source placed near a Geiger counter gives counts even in a dark, sealed box with no heating or pressure applied, showing that decay goes on by itself at its own rate.

18.9. What is meant by background radiations? Enlist some sources of background radiations.

Background radiations are the low level of nuclear radiations present everywhere all the time. Their sources are cosmic rays from space, radioactive rocks and soil (such as uranium and radon gas), building materials, food and water containing small amounts of radioactive potassium and carbon, and medical X-rays.

18.10. Describe two uses of radioisotopes in medicine, industry or research.

In medicine, iodine-131 is used to treat thyroid disease and technetium-99m is used for scans of the brain, thyroid, liver and kidneys. In industry, cobalt-60 gamma rays are used to sterilize medical equipment and food, and to check welds in pipes by radiography.

18.11. What are two common radiation hazards?

Briefly describe the precautions that are taken against them. Two hazards are damage to living cells, which can cause burns, sickness and cancer, and contamination of food, water and surfaces by radioactive material. Precautions are: keep the exposure time short, stay as far as possible from the source, use shielding such as lead screens, wear protective clothing and gloves, and never eat or drink near radioactive sources.

18.12. Complete this nuclear reaction: uranium-235 splits into xenon-140 (atomic number 54) + ? + 2 neutrons. Does this reaction involve fission or fusion? Justify your answer.

Balancing mass numbers: 235 = 140 + mass of unknown + 2, so the unknown mass number is 93. Balancing atomic numbers: 92 = 54 + atomic number of unknown, so it is 38, which is strontium-93. This is fission, because one heavy nucleus (uranium-235) splits into two lighter nuclei with the release of neutrons and energy.

18.13. Nuclear fusion reaction is more reliable and sustainable source of energy than nuclear fission chain reaction. Justify this statement with plausible arguments.

Fusion uses light nuclei such as hydrogen, which are abundant in seawater, so fuel is almost unlimited, while fission fuel (uranium) is limited. Fusion produces mainly harmless helium and very little long-lived radioactive waste, whereas fission produces dangerous waste that lasts thousands of years. Fusion is also safer because it stops by itself if conditions fail, while a fission chain reaction must be controlled to avoid accidents.

18.14. A nitrogen nuclide (nitrogen-14, atomic number 7) decays to become an oxygen nuclide by emitting an electron. Show this process with an equation.

Emitting an electron is beta decay, in which a neutron becomes a proton: mass number stays 14 while atomic number rises from 7 to 8. The equation is: nitrogen-14 changes into oxygen-14 plus an electron (beta particle). The parent is nitrogen-14 and the daughter is oxygen-14.

18.15. Determine which of these radioactive decay processes are possible: (a) polonium-214 changes into polonium-214 + alpha particle (b) thorium-230 changes into radium-226 + alpha particle (c) protactinium-233 changes into uranium-233 + beta particle (d) carbon-14 changes into nitrogen-14 + beta particle

(a) Not possible: mass and charge are not balanced, because an alpha particle is emitted without any change in the nucleus. (b) Possible: mass 230 = 226 + 4 and atomic number 90 = 88 + 2, both balanced. (c) Possible: beta decay keeps mass at 233 and raises atomic number from 91 to 92, which is exactly protactinium-233 changing into uranium-233. (d) Possible: carbon-14 (atomic number 6) decays to nitrogen-14 (atomic number 7) by beta emission, mass unchanged and atomic number increased by 1.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
18.1. Is it possible for an element to have different types of atoms? Explain.

Yes, an element can have different types of atoms called isotopes.

Isotopes have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers. For example, carbon has carbon-12 and carbon-14, both with 6 protons but with 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

18.2. What nuclear reaction would release more energy, the fission reaction or the fusion reaction? Explain.

Per unit mass of fuel, fusion releases more energy than fission. Fusing light nuclei into helium converts a larger fraction of mass into energy than splitting heavy nuclei, because the binding energy per nucleon is greatest near iron and the gain from light nuclei is larger. That is why the Sun's fusion gives out enormous energy from a small mass of hydrogen.

18.3. Which has more penetrating power, an alpha particle or a gamma ray photon?

A gamma ray photon has far more penetrating power than an alpha particle. Alpha particles are heavy and charged, so they lose energy quickly and are stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. Gamma rays have no charge or mass, so they pass through many centimetres of lead and can only be weakened, not fully stopped, by thick shielding.

18.4. What is the difference between natural and artificial radioactivity?

Natural radioactivity is the decay of unstable nuclei that occur in nature, such as uranium, radium and carbon-14, without human action. Artificial radioactivity is produced by humans by bombarding stable nuclei with particles in reactors or accelerators, creating new radioactive isotopes such as cobalt-60 and iodine-131 that do not occur naturally in large amounts.

18.5. How long would you likely have to wait to watch any sample of radioactive atoms completely decay?

In theory, you would have to wait an infinite time, because after each half-life half of what remains still survives. In practice, after about ten half-lives less than one-thousandth remains, which is usually too small to detect, so the sample is treated as fully decayed even though a few atoms may still remain.

18.6. Which type of natural radioactivity leaves the number of protons and the number of neutrons in the nucleus unchanged?

Gamma decay leaves both the number of protons and neutrons unchanged. The nucleus only loses energy by emitting a gamma photon and drops from an excited state to a lower energy state, with no change in mass number or atomic number.

18.7. How much of a 1 g sample of pure radioactive substance would be left undecayed after four half-lives?

After one half-life 1/2 g remains, after two 1/4 g, after three 1/8 g, and after four half-lives 1/16 g remains. So 1/16 of 1 g = 0.0625 g would be left undecayed after four half-lives.

18.8. Tritium (hydrogen-3) is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen. It decays by emitting an electron. What is the daughter nucleus?

Tritium decays by beta emission: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic number rises from 1 to 2 while mass number stays 3. The daughter nucleus is helium-3, with 2 protons and 1 neutron.

18.9. What information about the structure of the nitrogen atom can be obtained from its nuclide nitrogen-14 (atomic number 7)? In what way is the atom in nitrogen-14 different from the atom in nitrogen-16?

Nitrogen-14 has 7 protons and 14 - 7 = 7 neutrons, with 7 electrons in a neutral atom. Nitrogen-16 has the same 7 protons and 7 electrons but 16 - 7 = 9 neutrons, so it is a different isotope of nitrogen with two extra neutrons and a larger mass.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
18.1. The half-life of nitrogen-16 is 7.3 s. A sample of this nuclide of nitrogen is observed for 29.2 s. Calculate the fraction of the original radioactive isotope remaining after this time.

Step 1: Number of half-lives = time / half-life = 29.2 / 7.3 = 4.

Step 2: Fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16.

Final answer: Fraction remaining = 1/16.

18.2. Cobalt-60 is a radioactive element with half-life of 5.25 years. What fraction of the original sample will be left after 26 years?

Step 1: Number of half-lives = 26 / 5.25 = 4.95, about 5.

Step 2: Fraction remaining = (1/2)^5 = 1/32.

Final answer: Fraction remaining = 1/32 (book answer).

18.3. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. How long will it take for the quantity of carbon-14 in a sample to drop to one-eighth of the initial quantity?

Step 1: One-eighth = (1/2)^3, so 3 half-lives are needed.

Step 2: Time = 3 x 5730 = 17,190 years = 1.72 x 10^4 years.

Final answer: Time = 1.72 x 10^4 years.

18.4. Technetium-99m is a radioactive element used to diagnose brain, thyroid, liver and kidney diseases. This element has half-life of 6 hours. If there is 200 mg of this technetium present, how much will be left in 36 hours?

Step 1: Number of half-lives = 36 / 6 = 6.

Step 2: Amount remaining = 200 x (1/2)^6 = 200 / 64 = 3.125 mg.

Final answer: Amount left = 3.12 mg.

18.5. Half-life of a radioactive element is 10 minutes. If the initial count rate is 368 counts per minute, find the time for which count rate reaches 23 counts per minute.

Step 1: 368 to 23 is a factor of 368/23 = 16 = 2^4, so 4 half-lives pass.

Step 2: Time = 4 x 10 = 40 minutes.

Final answer: Time = 40 minutes.

18.6. In an experiment to measure the half-life of a radioactive element, the following results were obtained: count rate per minute 400, 200, 100, 50, 25 at times 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 minutes. Plot a graph between the count rate and time in minutes. Measure the value for the half-life of the element from the graph.

Step 1: Plot count rate on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis; the points form a falling curve.

Step 2: The count rate halves from 400 to 200 in 2 minutes, from 200 to 100 in the next 2 minutes, and so on.

Step 3: The time for the count rate to fall to half its value is therefore 2 minutes at every step.

Final answer: Half-life = 2 minutes.

18.7. A sample of certain radioactive element has a half-life of 1500 years. If it has an activity of 32000 counts per hour at the present time, plot a graph of the activity of this sample over the period in which it will reduce to 1/16 of its present value.

Step 1: 1/16 = (1/2)^4, so 4 half-lives are needed: 4 x 1500 = 6000 years.

Step 2: Activities: at 0 years 32000; at 1500 years 16000; at 3000 years 8000; at 4500 years 4000; at 6000 years 2000 counts per hour.

Step 3: Plot these points with time on the horizontal axis and activity on the vertical axis, joining them with a smooth falling curve.

Final answer: Activity falls to 2000 counts per hour (1/16 of present) after 6000 years.

18.8. Half-life of a radioactive element was found to be 4000 years. The count rates per minute for 8 successive hours were found to be 270, 280, 300, 310, 285, 290, 305, 312. What does the variation in count rates show? Plot a graph between the count rates and time in hours. Why the graph is a straight line rather than an exponential?

Step 1: The small up-and-down variation (270 to 312) around a mean of about 295 shows the random nature of radioactive decay.

Step 2: Plotted against time, the points form an almost horizontal straight line, not a falling curve.

Step 3: This is because the half-life (4000 years) is enormously longer than the 8-hour observation period, so the activity hardly falls at all in 8 hours.

Final answer: Variation shows random decay; graph is almost horizontal because the half-life is very long compared with 8 hours.

18.9. Ashes from a campfire deep in a cave show carbon-14 activity of only one-eighth the activity of fresh wood. How long ago was that campfire made?

Step 1: One-eighth = (1/2)^3, so 3 half-lives have passed.

Step 2: Half-life of carbon-14 = 5730 years. Time = 3 x 5730 = 17,190 years.

Final answer: The campfire was made 17,190 years ago.
